Ocasio-Cortez wants more environmental politicians in Congress. She called climate change "the single biggest national security threat" for the United States and the world". With the United Nations saying that the effects of climate change cannot be fixed until carbon emissions are slowed down in the next 12 years. She said that the younger generation would suffer from the effects of climate change. Ocasio-Cortez supports ending the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency. She compared the agency to the Patriot Act and to a paramilitary-like agency. In June 2018, she said she would support ending the agency and she would rather "create a pathway to citizenship for more immigrants through decriminalization." She later said that this does not mean ending all deportations. Two days before the primary election, she went to a protest at an ICE child-detention center in Tornillo, Texas. She was the only Democrat to vote against H.R. 648, a bill to fund and reopen the government, because it would give more federal money to ICE. Ocasio-Cortez supports moving to a single-payer health care system. She said that medical care is a human right. In September 2019, she created an anti-poverty policy proposal that would make the cost of childcare, healthcare, and "new necessities" like Internet access when measuring poverty. The proposal would stop rent prices going higher and create better ways for people with convictions and immigrants to have social welfare programs. Ocasio-Cortez is a supporter of LGBTQ rights and equality. She has said she supports the LGBTQ community and thanked its members for their role in her campaign. In January 2019, she gave a speech in support of laws needed to keep LGBTQ rights in jobs and everywhere in the country. She also supports transgender rights and said that "trans rights are civil rights". Ocasio-Cortez has been supportive of Puerto Rico. Ocasio-Cortez did not approve of the Federal Emergency Management Agency's response to Hurricane Maria. She believes the federal government should pay more attention to Puerto Rico. Ocasio-Cortez has been against wars during her time in congress. In 2025, she was against American strikes on Iranian nuclear sites, saying it was "absolutely and clearly grounds for impeachment". That same year, she supported the "Block the Bombs Act", which would stop the U.S. from giving Israel multiple weapons. The MIT Lincoln Laboratory named the asteroid 23238 Ocasio-Cortez after her when she was a senior in high school because she finished in second-place in the 2007 Intel International Science and Engineering Fair. She was named the 2017 National Hispanic Institute Person of the Year by Ernesto Nieto. In 2019, She received the Adelle Foley Award. She was named as one of the 2019 BBC 100 Women. After the death of Ocasio-Cortez's father in 2008, her mother and grandmother moved to Florida because of money problems. She still has family in Puerto Rico, where her grandfather was living in a nursing home before he died during Hurricane Maria. Ocasio-Cortez talked about her Catholic faith and why it is important for her life and her campaign for criminal justice reform in an article she wrote for America. At a December 2018 Hanukkah celebration in New York, she said that she has Jewish ancestry, although she does not practice Judaism. During the 2018 election campaign, Ocasio-Cortez lived in Parkchester, Bronx, with her boyfriend, web developer Riley Roberts. In April 2022, Ocasio-Cortez became engaged to Roberts. In August 2026, it was announced that Ocasio-Cortez and Roberts had ended their engagement in 2024. In 2019, Ocasio-Cortez was named as one of the 2019 BBC 100 Women. In 2020, Ocasio-Cortez was a guest judge on an episode of RuPaul's Drag Race. In February 2021, Ocasio-Cortez said that she was a sexual assault survivor when asked about how she felt during the 2021 storming of the United States Capitol. That same year in May, Ocasio-Cortez said that she has been in psychotherapy because of the events of the United States Capitol. She said she "did not know if I was going to make it to the end of that day alive". In 2022, she said that she was raped by her then-boyfriend about ten years ago. In March 2021, Ocasio-Cortez was name one of the least wealthy members of the Congress, with a net worth of $30,000.

Alexios I Komnenos or Alexius I Comnenus (Αλέξιος Α' Κομνηνός, Alexios I Komnēnos; ALEXIVS I COMNENVS; 1048 – August 15, 1118), Byzantine emperor (1081–1118), was the son of John Komnenos and Anna Dalassena. He was the nephew of Isaac I Komnenos (emperor 1057–1059). The military, financial and territorial recovery of the Byzantine Empire known as Komnenian restoration began in his time.

Alexey Ivanovich Kazannik (; 26 July 1941 – 2 June 2019) was a Russian lawyer and politician. He was born in Horodnia Raion, Ukrainian SSR. He studied law at Irkutsk State University and graduated in 1967. In 1989, he became known for giving his seat in the Supreme Soviet of the Soviet Union to Boris Yeltsin. From 1993 to 1994, Kazannik was Prosecutor General of Russia. Kazannik later served as Deputy Governor of Omsk Oblast from 1995 to 2003. He also taught law at Omsk State University. Kazannik died after a long illness on 2 June 2019 in Omsk. He was 77.

Alexey Ivanovich Sorokin (28 March 1922 – 4 March 2020) was a Soviet Admiral of the Fleet. He was a member of the Congress of People's Deputies of the Soviet Union. He was a political officer and studied at the Lenin Military-Political Academy between 1948 and 1952. Sorokin died on 4 March 2020 in Moscow at the age of 97. Order of the Patriotic War, 1st class, twice, and 2nd class Order for Service to the Homeland in the Armed Forces of the USSR, 3rd class Jubilee Medal "In Commemoration of the 100th Anniversary since the Birth of Vladimir Il'ich Lenin" Medal "For the Victory over Germany in the Great Patriotic War 1941–1945"
Alexis Galanos (, 30 August 1940 – 15 July 2019) was a Greek Cypriot politician. He was President of the House of Representatives of Cyprus from 1991 to 1996.

Alexander Giannoulias (; born March 16, 1976) is an American financier and politician who has been the 38th Illinois Secretary of State since 2023. Giannoulias ran as the Democratic nominee for Secretary of State in 2022. He was the 72nd Illinois Treasurer from 2007 to 2011. He is a Democrat. He was a candidate in the 2010 elections for the United States Senate, but lost to Republican Mark Kirk. In August 2026, Giannoulias announced his candidacy for mayor of Chicago in the 2027 election.

Alexey Spas (Алексей Спас; born 30 November 1977) is a business executive and software engineer. He is the co-founder and chief executive officer of Instinctools, a software development company. Spas was born on 30 November 1977 in Hrodna, then part of the Byelorussian Soviet Socialist Republic. In 1999, he graduated from the Yanka Kupala State University of Grodno, Faculty of Physics and Engineering. In 2006, he received a Master of Business Administration from Pforzheim University, specialising in international management. While still a student, Spas began working as a software developer. In 2000, he co-founded Instinctools together with Diethard Sohn as a software development company. The company, which operates under the stylised name Instinctools, grew from a local startup into an international technology firm. In 2009, Spas co-founded and developed DITA webtop (later branded as DITAworks Webtop), a software-as-a-service platform for enterprise technical documentation management. In November 2011, Spas presented on Eclipse-based product development at the DISCOVER IT Belarus seminar held at the Maritim Hotel in Munich. In September 2024, Spas represented Instinctools at the Forrester Technology & Innovation Summit in Austin, Texas, where the company participated as a Silver Sponsor. Together with Chad West, Managing Director at Instinctools USA, he introduced an AI-powered conversational chatbot designed for enterprise business communication. Instinctools has organised an annual Christmas charity initiative in collaboration with its clients, which has been covered in the company's news publications. In 2026, Spas joined the Forbes Technology Council, a professional community for senior technology executives.

Alf Ivar Samuelsen (28 February 1942 – 16 September 2014) was a Norwegian politician for the Centre Party. Samuelsen served as Mayor of Flakstad. He served as mayor from 1986 through 1987. Samuelsen was born in Flakstad. He was elected to the Parliament of Norway from Nordland in 2005. He was not re-elected in 2009. Samuelsen died in a tractor accident on 16 September 2014 in Flakstad. He was 72.

Alexis Tsipras (,; born 28 July 1974) is a Greek politician. He served as the Leader of the Opposition from 2019 to 2023 and as president of Syriza from 2009 to 2023. He was Prime Minister of Greece from 2015 to 2019. Tsipras has been described as a democratic socialist. A major issue of his term has been dealing with the Greek debt crisis.

Alfred Mossman Landon (September 9, 1887 – October 12, 1987) was an American politician. He was a member of the Republican Party. He served as the 26th Governor of Kansas from 1933 to 1937. Landon was the Republican Party’s nominee in the 1936 presidential election, but was defeated in a landslide by incumbent President Franklin D. Roosevelt. President Reagan and Mrs. Reagan attended Landon's hundredth birthday party at his home in Topeka. President Reagan described Landon as "the living soul of Kansas" and remarked, "You don't know what a joy it is to come to a birthday party of someone who in all honesty can call me a kid." His daughter was U.S. Senator Nancy Kassebaum.

Alexis Charles-Henri-Maurice Clérel, Viscount de Tocqueville (;; 29 July 180516 April 1859) was a French diplomat, political scientist and historian. He was best known for his works Democracy in America (appearing in two volumes, 1835 and 1840) and The Old Regime and the Revolution. Tocqueville was born in July 29, 1805 in Paris, France to a political family. His great grandfather, Chrétien de Malesherbes, was his political model and his father was a loyal royalist prefect and became a peer of France by King Charles X in 1827. As a young man, he became an apprentice magistrate. Preparing for his career in politics, he observed confrontations between the Conservatives and Liberals. François Guizot's lectures was a huge influence on him. He also became a close friend of Gustave de Beaumont. The 1830 July Revolution had a huge impact on Tocqueville. He believed that France is moving towards social equality. His nine-month visit to the United States, along with his friend Beaumont, in 1831 and 1832 created some of Tocqueville's famous work, the first part of the Democracy in America in 1835. This work made him famous as a political scientist. In 1836, he married Mary Mottley and published the final portion of the Democracy in America in 1840. In 1839, he was elected deputy from Valognes and was elected to the new legislative Assembly under France's Second Republic. He was appointed as Minister of Foreign Affairs. Beginning in 1850, he suffered from tuberculosis. He wrote his recollections and reflections such as those on the February Revolution. It was published in July 1851. As one of the representatives who opposed the coup d'etat by Louis-Napoleon, he was imprisoned. After his imprisonment, he retired from politics and make studies for his work, The Old Regime and the Revolution, published in January 1856. He then relocated to Cannes in October 1858. Six months later, he died on April 1859. In the United States, Tocqueville believed that abolition did not eliminate racism, segregation, or hatred between black and white people. He predicted that this would weaken American democracy. In the French Caribbean, he suggested that the French learn from the English experience of abolition. He believed that successful abolition required legal changes and changes in attitudes. Tocqueville was an admirer of democracy particularly in the United States. He was impressed by Americans' industriousness, resourcefulness, and ability to form voluntary associations to solve problems. He believed that democracy in America was not just about voting or laws but also about a mindset that valued personal initiative, social equality, and a commitment to public service. However, he was criticized for his views about the downside of popular governance by the masses or what he called as "tyranny of the majority". Tocqueville argued that in a democratic society where the majority rules, there is a risk that the majority's opinions and preferences could become so big and dominant that the rights of minorities to speak their voices are not important or not really relevant for the most part. He also studied a lot and found that many of the problems France had after the revolution were similar to the problems they had before. These were published in his book The Old Regime and the Revolution (1856). He believed that France was stuck in the past and wasn't as democratic as he had hoped. However, he was encouraged by the example of the United States, which was more democratic and free.

Alfonso Daniel (30 January 1886 – 7 January 1950), also known as Castelao, was a Spanish writer on Galician language and one of the main symbols of Galicia. As a politician, caricaturist, and writer, he is one of the leading figures of Galician culture and identity. In 1886, Alfonso Daniel Rodríguez de Castelao was born on 30 January in Rianxo, Galicia, Spain. Castelao spent his childhood and adolescence in Santa Rosa de Toay, Argentina. In 1900, the Castelao family returned to Rianxo. In 1908, he obtained his degree in Medicine from the University of Santiago de Compostela. The next year, he passed his doctorate in Madrid, where he started to become known as a caricaturist, and settled down in Rianxo, joining the political movement Action Galicia (Acción Gallega in Spanish). As a caricaturist, Castelao focussed on the everyday in a humorous way, although after the cruelty and tragedy of the Spanish Civil War, he turned to using his art to denounce the misery of Fascism. In 1916, he moved to Pontevedra, where he joined the Irmandades da Fala and participated in the Asembleia Nazonalista de Lugo, signing an important national declaration. In 1920, he became editor of the magazine Nos and travelled through France, the Netherlands and Germany. In 1922, he wrote the novel Un Ollo de Vidro and in 1924 he joined the Seminario de Estudos Galegos and founded the Coral Polifonica de Pontevedra. Two years later he published Cousas, and in 1929 he travelled to Brittany to study its stone crosses and publish As Cruces de Pedra na Bretaña.

Alfonso García Robles (20 March 1911 – 2 September 1991) was a Mexican diplomat and politician. García Robles received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1982, together with Sweden's Alva Myrdal. García Robles was the driving force behind the Treaty of Tlatelolco. This treaty established a nuclear-free zone in Latin America and the Caribbean.

Pablo Alfonso Espinosa of the Monteros Rueda (born 24 December 1941) is an Ecuadorian news anchor and vice-president of news of Ecuavisa in Quito. He holds the Guinness World Record for "Longest career as Television News broadcaster". Espinosa de los Monteros was born on 24 December 1941 in Quito, Ecuador. His parents were from Ibarra. Espinosa de los Monteros worked for different radio stations in the cities of Ibarra and Guayaquil until 1962. In 1963 he was news director for Radio La Prensa. He began in Ecuavisa in 1967, the year of its foundation, as the first news anchor of the station. He was News Director for almost three decades. He hosted the Ecuadorian version of "Who wants to be millionaire" (2001 - 2004 and 2009 - 2011). He received the “Honorato Vázquez” medal from the Ecuadorian government in 1992. On 1 May 2023, Espinosa de los Monteros retired from Ecuavisa after 56 years. In August 2014, he obtained the Guinness World Record for "Longest career as Television News broadcaster”.

Alfons "Fons" Remi Emiel Viscount Verplaetse (19 February 1930 – 15 October 2020) was a Belgian economist. He was Governor of the National Bank of Belgium (NBB) from 1989 until 1999. He was one of the main people that helped the creation Belgian Frank in 1982. He worked at the cabinet of Wilfried Martens. Verplaetse was born in Zulte, Belgium. Verplaetse died of COVID-19 on 15 October 2020 in Brussels, aged 90.

Alfonso Gagliano (; (January 25, 1942 – December 12, 2020) was an Italian-born Canadian accountant and a Liberal Party politician. He was born in Siculiana, Italy. Gagliano was a member of the Parliament of Canada from 1984 to 2002. He also was a Minister of Labour from 1996 to 1997 and of Public Works and Government Services from 1997 to 2002. Gagliano died on December 12, 2020 at the age of 78.

Alfhild was a daughter of the Geatish king Synardus that lived in modern Sweden. Historians do not know if she was a real person or a legend. If she did live, it was probably between the 5th and 12th centuries. The earliest piece of writing that talks about her is the Gesta Danorum. When Alfhild was a young princess, the room she slept in was guarded by a lizard and a snake. These reptiles scared away suitors who were not brave. A Danish prince named Alf, who was also Geatish, came to Geatland and fought the animal guards and won. But Alfhild's mother told her to run away from Alf dressed as a man. She did, and she became a woman fighter called a shield maiden. She found a group of pirate ships that had lost their captain. She became the captain and made the other women part of the sailing crew. The crew doubled in number. She was so good at piracy that she hurt a large part of the Danish and Finnish shipping economy. She also sailed to Iceland once. Prince Alf then went to stop the fleet. At that time, he did not know that Alfhild was pirate leader. He found them off the coast of Finland. In the original story, Alfhild killed Alf, the latter underestimating the fleet's power, and then put his head on a spear and continued pirating. People know this from Norse hearsay in dining halls. In Christian story, she knocked off his helmet. This made her recognize him, and she stopped pirating and married Alf. She then became queen of Denmark. This version is probably wrong: It agreed with the things Christianity and patriarchy saw as good. There are some differences in the story in later popular culture. Here Alfhild is almost always called Awilda. (Other spellings: Alwilda, Alvilda, Alvild, Alvilde, Alfhilda, Avilda, Alvida, Altilda, Ælfhild). During the 1800s, Alfhild/Awilda was a popular subject for scrimshaw carved by sailors on whaling ships. The story about Alf And Alfhild has also been made into Italian operas. In 1686, "L'Amazzone Corsara, ovvero L'Alvilda, regina de Goti", by Carlo Pallavicino.

Alfonso Márquez de la Plata Yrarrázaval (19 July 1933 – 22 April 2014) was a Chilean politician, businessman and writer. He was Minister of Agriculture from 1977 until 1980. He was later the Ministry General Secretariat of Government from 1983 to 1984. He was born in Santiago. Márquez died from pneumonia on 22 April 2014 in Santiago. He was 80.

Alfonso VII (1 March 1105 – 21 August 1157), born Alfonso Raimúndez, he was called the Emperor (el Emperador). He was given rule in Galacia alongside his mother Urraca of León in 1107. Alfonso became the King of Galicia in 1111. He became King of León and Castile in 1126 after his mother's death. Alfonso adopted the style of Emperor in his charters. In 1135 in a ceremony at the court of Leon he was officially recognize as Emperor. He was the son of Urraca of León and Raymond of Burgundy. He was the first of the House of Burgundy to rule in the Iberian peninsula. During his rule Portugal declared independence, in 1128. It was recognized as being independent in 1143.

Alfonso La Marmora (18 November 1804 – 5 January 1878), or Alfonso Ferrero La Marmora, Alfonso Lamarmora and Alfonso Ferrero, Cavaliere La Marmora, was an Italian general and statesman. He was born at Turin in a rich and noble family: his father was a Marquis. In 1822 he graduated in the Military Academy of Turin; then began a military career, which led him to become general in 1856. In the Kingdom of Sardinia he was twice Minister of War in the governments led by Massimo D'Azeglio and Camillo Cavour. In 1854 La Marmora made a law that improved the quality of the troops, created new academies for officers, retouched the recruitment system, bringing to 60,000 Army soldiers (of which only a quarter in active service, while the rest evaded the lever paying a substitute), doubled the units of riflemen and strengthened the light cavalry at the expense of heavy. Even the artillery, health and administrative apparatus were renovated, as well as logistics services. In 1855 he resigned from the post of Minister of War because he went to fight in the Crimean War. He was Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Sardinia from 19 July 1859 to 21 January 1860. In the years immediately after the Italian unification, he was governor of Milan and Prefect of Naples. Member of the "Historical Right", La Marmora was Prime Minister and Foreign Minister of the Kingdom of Italy from 18 September 1864 to 20 July 1866. He resigned from office to go fight the third Italian independence war: on this occasion, however, he committed several strategic errors, which cost a heavy defeat for Italy. In 1870 he retired from political life. He died in Florence and was buried in Biella in the church of San Sebastiano. His brother, Alessandro La Marmora, founded the corps of Bersaglieri.

Alfonso López Michelsen (30 June 1913 – 11 July 2007) was the 24th President of Colombia from 1974 to 1978. López was the son of former two time president of Colombia, Alfonso López Pumarejo. He was born and raised in Bogotá. In 1974, López was selected by the Liberal Party in as their candidate for president after defeating former president Carlos Lleras Restrepo in the party presidential primaries. He won the general election by a large margin against the Conservative Party candidate Álvaro Gómez Hurtado and the ANAPO candidate, María Eugenia Rojas. In his inaugural speech on August 7, 1974, López was mostly remembered for calling the border disputed area in the Gulf of Venezuela by its native name "Gulf of Coquibacoa" given by the wayuus. On September 14, 1977 in Bogotá a bloody riot started in all sections of the city, the riot was called The National Civic Strike. The two days riot left a death toll of 80 people, and 2000 people injured. Upon the end of his term in 1978, he again became the leader of Liberal Party. He ran for president again in 1982, but was defeated by the Conservative Party candidate, Belisario Betancur. Lopez Michelsen died in Bogotá on July 11, 2007 after suffering a heart attack.

Alfonso XIII (17 May 1886 – 28 February 1941), also known as El Africano or the African, was King of Spain from 17 May 1886 to 14 April 1931, the monarchy was abolished when the Second Republic was proclaimed.

Alfonso IX (15 August 1171 — 24 September 1230) nicknamed the Warrior King was King of León and Galicia from in 1188 until his death in 1230. During his reign, León became more powerful and modern. He founded the University of Salamanca in 1212. Alfonso improved relations with the Catholic Church and the pope. He was also a great warrior. He actively fought in the Reconquista, conquering several territories within Extremadura, capturing Mérida and Badajoz in 1230 before he died later that year at the age of 59. He was succeeded by his son who already ruled Castile, Ferdinand III, who successfully united León with Castile.

Alfonso XI (13 August 1311 – 26 October 1350) nicknamed the Avenger was the King of Castile and León from 1312 until his death in 1350. His long 38-year reign was one of the most successful in the history of Castile. Like his predecessors, Alfonso was very active in the Reconquista. He conquered Granadans and Marinids after his victory at the Battle of Río Salado in 1340. He also gained control over the Strait of Gibraltar. Alfonso became king after the death of his father, King Ferdinand IV, in 1312 where Alfonso was only one-year old at the time. During Alfonso's minority, 6 people held the regency: Constance of Portugal, Alfonso's mother, Peter, Lord of Cameros, Alfonso's uncle, John, Lord of Valencia de Campos, Alfonso's granduncle, María de Molina, Alfonso's grandmother, and Philip, Lord of Cabrera and Ribera, Alfonso's other uncle and the brother of Peter. On Alfonso's 14th birthday on 13 August 1325, he was crowned and his effective rule began. He was a very strong king as he made many successes in the Reconquista. He was also very popular among the Castilians as well as at the end of his rule, Castile was thriving and was one of the most powerful kingdoms in the Iberian Peninsula. During his rule, the Black Death strucked Europe as well. Alfonso died as a result of the pandemic on 26 October 1350 in Gibraltar at the age of 39. He was succeeded by his 16-year old son, Peter.

Alfonso de Galarreta (born 14 January 1957) is a Spanish traditionalist Catholic bishop. He is a member and leader in the Society of Saint Pius X (SSPX). He was excommunicated (excluded) from the Catholic Church two times after he helped to consecrate new bishops without the permission of the pope. Alfonso de Galarreta was born on 14 January 1957 in Torrelavega, Spain. When he was young, his family moved to Argentina. In 1975, he started to study at a seminary in La Plata. In 1978, he moved to the International Seminary of Saint Pius X in Écône, Switzerland. In 1980, Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre ordained him as a priest in Buenos Aires. After that, Galarreta worked as a teacher at an SSPX seminary in La Reja, Argentina. From 1985 to 1988, he was the leader of the SSPX in South America. On 30 June 1988, Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre consecrated (officially made a bishop in a religious ceremony) Galarreta as a bishop. Pope John Paul II did not give permission for this ceremony. Because of this, the Catholic Church automatically excommunicated Galarreta. Galarreta said that this excommunication was not valid. In January 2009, Pope Benedict XVI lifted (ended) this first excommunication. However, Galarreta was still suspended from his religious work by Rome. In 2018, he was chosen as the First Assistant General under the new SSPX leader, Davide Pagliarani. On 1 July 2026, Bishop Galarreta consecrated four new SSPX priests as bishops in Écône, Switzerland. These new bishops were Pascal Schreiber, Michael Goldade, Michel Poinsinet de Sivry, and Marc Hanappier. Pope Leo XIV did not agree to these consecrations and asked the SSPX to stop. Because Galarreta consecrated them without a papal mandate, he was automatically excommunicated for the second time under canon law.

Alfred William Deakin (3 August 1856 – 7 October 1919) was the second Prime Minister of Australia. He was the prime minister three times: 1903 to 1904, 1905 to 1908 and 1909 to 1910. He was born in Collingwood, Melbourne, Australia, the second child of William Deakin. In the 1890s he helped Australia become a country. He was Australia's first Attorney-General (head lawyer) when Edmund Barton was Prime Minister and then became Prime Minister after Barton left. He introduced the Bill to start Australia's High Court, began planning for a railway to cross Australia, took over control of New Guinea from Britain, and introduced old age pensions. Deakin married Elizabeth Brown on 3 April 1882. They had three children. When he was old he had Alzheimer's disease which made him forget a lot of things. Alfred Deakin died on the 7 October 1919 in South Yarra, Victoria. He was buried at St.Kilda Cemetery.

Alfred Dreyfus (9 October 1859 – 12 July 1935) was a French officer of Jewish descent. He was wrongly accused of treason against the French military. This scandal was known as the Dreyfus affair. He was imprisoned on Devil's Island in French Guiana. His highest rank was lieutenant colonel. Dreyfus was born in Mulhouse and died in Paris.

Alfred Gusenbauer (born February 8, 1960, in St. Pölten, Austria) was the chancellor of Austria from January 2007 to December 2008. His party won the elections of 2008, and he was succeeded as Chancellor the new party leader, Werner Faymann, on 2 December 2008. He was the leader of the political party SPÖ.

Alfred Thambirajah Duraiappah (died 27 July 1975) was a Sri Lankan politician. He was a Member of Parliament and mayor of Jaffna. He was assassinated by the Tamil Tigers. Alfred Duraiappah was a member of the Sri Lanka Freedom Party. He became a Member of Parliament and mayor of Jaffna. He was murdered by the Tamil Tiger leader Velupillai Prabhakaran in July 1975. Duraiappah was killed on his way to a Hindu temple for prayers, although he himself was a Christian. His term as the mayor of a neglected city. Roads and stadiums were built, and jobs were created. His period of office also saw benefits for Jaffna farmers, as the prices of agriculture grew, possibly because the government policies taking control at the time was beneficial.

Alfred Cotton Bedford (November 5, 1863 - September 21, 1925) was president of the Standard Oil Company of New Jersey starting on December 22, 1916. Bedford was born on November 5, 1863 in Brooklyn, New York City. He married Edith Kinsman Clark on January 8, 1890. He was promoted from treasurer to president of the Standard Oil Company of New Jersey starting on December 22, 1916. He was made chairman of the board on November 15, 1917. He was made a Commandant of the Legion in 1922. Bedford died on September 21, 1925 leaving an estate of $3,000,000. He was buried in Green-Wood Cemetery in Brooklyn.

Alfred Gadenne (31 January 1946 in Luingne – 11 September 2017 in Luingne) was a Belgian politician. He was a member of the Centre démocrate humaniste and Mayor of Mouscron in Hainaut from 2006 until his death in September 2017. Gadenne was found dead on 11 September 2017 at the age of 71 after having his throat slashed at a graveyard close to his home in Mouscron. Local news report a suspect had handed himself in to police. The suspect is an 18 years inhabitant of Mouscron. He murdered Gadenne because his father (a fireman) had committed suicide after being fired by Gadenne. Gadenne was an alderman of Mouscron from 1982 to 2006. He was also a member of the Parliament of Wallonia and the Parliament of the French Community from 2009 to 2014.

Alfred Gomolka (21 July 1942 – 24 March 2020) was a German politician. He was a Member of the European Parliament for Mecklenburg-Vorpommern from 1994 to 2008. He was a member of the conservative Christian Democratic Union of Germany, part of the European People's Party. He was the first Minister President of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern from 1990 to 1992 and was the President of the Bundesrat from 1 November 1991 to 19 March 1992. Gomolka died on 24 March 2020 from a fall in Schwerin, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, aged 77.

Nnaemeka Alfred Achebe, CFR (born 14 May 1941), popularly called Agbogidi is a Nigerian traditional ruler who serves as the 21st and current Obi of Onitsha, a city in Anambra State since 2002. As an Academian, Achebe became the chancellor of Ahmadu Bello University since 2015 after previously being the chancellor of Kogi State University. Achebe had worked as the chairman of the board of Directors of Unilever Nigeria until his retirement in 2023. He was also the chairman of International Breweries, Nigeria, Director of Royal Dutch Shell Group and others.

Alfred Hugh Kingon (born May 11, 1931) is an American businessman who was the White House Cabinet Secretary under President Ronald Reagan from 1985 to 1987. He also was the United States Ambassador to the European Union from 1987 to 1989.

Alfred Goshaw is an American physicist and professor emeritus at Duke University whose research focuses on experimental elementary particle physics research in collaborations at Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL), Fermilab (FNAL) and CERN.. He is recipient of High Energy and Particle Physics Prize and a fellow of American Physical Society. Goshaw earned a Bachelor of Science in electrical engineering from the University of Wisconsin–Madison in 1959 and continued at the same institution for graduate study, receiving a Ph.D. in physics in 1966. He subsequently held a postdoctoral position in physics at Princeton University from 1966 to 1969. After his postdoctoral work, Goshaw spent four years as physicist on the staff at CERN from 1969 to 1973. He then joined the faculty of Duke University as an assistant professor of physics in 1973, becoming associate professor in 1978, full professor in 1984, and James B. Duke Professor in 2000. He continued teaching and conducting research at Duke until his retirement in 2020 when he became professor emeritus. After retirement from Duke he continues to do research at CERN with the ATLAS experiment. Goshaw’s research career spans the evolution of the Standard Model of elementary particle physics with experimental measurements in the1960’using bubble chambers to current research using large modern collider experiments

Alfred Pritchard Sloan, Jr. (May 23, 1875 – February 17, 1966) was the president and chairman of General Motors. Sloan was born in a business family. He passed the examination of Massachusetts Institute of Technology when he was very young. When he was 26 his father bought a bearing company and made him president. The company did well and Sloan became president of General Motors. He managed the company with a new combination of centralization and decentralization and led the company into prosperity. Besides, he was a philanthropist who donated considerable money to charity.

Alfred Wilhelm Franz Maria Hugenberg (19 June 1865 - 12 March 1951) was a German businessman and politician. He was also a member of Hitler's Cabinet in 1933. In 1933, he was the minister of food in Germany. Hugenberg was heading the German National People's Party (DNVP). During the period of the Weimar Republic and Nazi Germany he was a member of the Reichstag.

Alfred Josef Ferdinand Jodl (10 May 1890 in Würzburg – 16 October 1946 in Nuremberg) was a German military Officer and commander. He was the Chief of the Operations Staff of the Armed Forces High Command (Oberkommando der Wehrmacht, or OKW) during World War II. At the Nuremberg trials he was tried, sentenced to death and hanged as a war criminal. Jodl joined the Imperial German Army in 1910 as a Army Infantry Soldier until 1912 when he became a junior Military Army Officer. He remained as a Junior Officer in the Reichswehr German Army until he became a Senior Officer in the Wehrmacht German Army in 1936 where he remained as a Senior officer until 1945.

Alfred Spiro Moisiu (; born 1 December 1929) is an Albanian politician. He was the fourth President of the Republic of Albania from 2002–2007. He is the eldest son of famed Albanian Army general Spiro Moisiu. Knight Grand Cross of the Croatian Grand Order of King Tomislav (, July 2, 2007), "For outstanding contribution to the promotion of friendship and development co-operation between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Albania." Grand Cross of the Order of Vytautas the Great (27 March 2007) Honorary Knight Grand Cross of the Order of St Michael and St George

Alfred Miodowicz (June 28, 1929 – September 17, 2021) was a Polish politician and trade union activist. He was born in Poznań, Poland. Miodowicz was a member of communist Polish United Workers Party. He held posts in the State National Council, Central Committee and Political Bureau. He was also the leader of the All-Poland Alliance of Trade Unions and took part in the Polish Round Table Agreement. Miodowicz died on September 17, 2021 at the age of 92.

Alfred Mason Gray Jr. (June 22, 1928 – March 20, 2024) was a United States Marine Corps general. He served as the 29th Commandant of the Marine Corps from 1987 to 1991. He retired from the U.S. Marine Corps in 1991 after 41 years of service. General Gray was promoted to general and became Commandant of the Marine Corps on July 1, 1987. His appointment as Commandant of the Marine Corps was recommended by Jim Webb, then Secretary of the Navy. Gray died at his home in Alexandria, Virginia on March 20, 2024, at the age of 95.

Alfred Pleasonton (July 7, 1824 – February 17, 1897) was a United States Army officer and major general of volunteers in the Union cavalry. This was during the American Civil War. He led the Cavalry Corps of the Army of the Potomac during the Gettysburg Campaign. This would also include the biggest cavalry battle of the war, Brandy Station. Pleasonton was born in Washington, D.C., on July 7, 1824.

Alfred Kolleritsch (16 February 1931 – 29 May 2020) was an Austrian people journalist, poet and philosopher. He was born in Eichfeld, Austria. He was the founder of the literary magazine manuscripts. He was the President of the Forum Stadtpark, a cultural center in Graz. Kolleritsch died on 29 May 2020 in Graz, aged 89.

Alfred Muller (23 December 1940 – 13 November 2020), was a French politician. He was a member of the National Assembly of France from 1993 to 1997. He also was the Mayor of Schiltigheim from 1977 to 2008. He was born in Strasbourg, France. He was a member of the Socialist Party. Muller died on 13 November 2020 at the age of 79.

Alfred Mayer (5 March 1936 – 1 March 2022) was an Austrian politician. He was a member of the Austrian People's Party. He was a Landesrat of Vorarlberg from 1974 to 1993. Mayer was born in Bregenz, Vorarlberg, Austria. Mayer died on 1 March 2022, at the age of 85.

Alfred Marie-Jeanne (; born 15 November 1936) is a French politician. He is known as a leader in the Martinican Independence Movement (MIM), starting in 1978. He was mayor of the commune of Rivière-Pilote from 1971 to 2000 and was President of the Regional Council of Martinique from March 20, 1998, to March 22, 2010. Marie-Jeanne represented Martinique's 1st constituency in the French National Assembly from 2012 to 2017.

Alfredo Baquerizo Moreno (28 September 1859, in Guayaquil – 20 March 1951) was an Ecuadorian politician. He served as Vice President of Ecuador of Leónidas Plaza and Lizardo García from 1903 to 1906 and as President of Ecuador three times in August - September 1912, September 1916 – August 1920 and October 1931 - August 1932. He was a member of the Ecuadorian Radical Liberal Party.

Alfredo Biondi (June 29, 1928 – June 24, 2020) was an Italian politician and lawyer. In 1994 he served as Minister of Justice of the Italian Republic during the first cabinet chaired by Silvio Berlusconi. He was also Minister of the Environment in the Bettino Craxi cabinet from 1983 to 1984. Until 1994, he was a member of the Liberal Party. Afterwards, he became a member of Forza Italia. Biondi was born in Pisa, Italy. He was a Deputy from 1968 to 1972 and again from 1979 to 2006. Biondi was a Senator from 2006 to 2008. Biondi died on June 24, 2020 in Genoa, Italy at the age of 91.

Alfred Sant (born 28 February 1948) is a Maltese politician and a novelist. He led the Labour Party from 1992 to 2008. He served as Prime Minister of Malta between 1996 and 1998 and as Leader of the Opposition from 1992 to 1996 and from 1998 to 2008.

Alfredo Félix Cristiani Burkard, popularly known as Alfredo Cristiani (born November 22, 1947) is a Peruvian politician. He was the President of El Salvador from 1989 to 1994. Cristiani was born in San Salvador. He is a member of the ARENA. Cristiani is of Swiss decent.

Alfred Merrill Worden (February 7, 1932 – March 18, 2020) was an American astronaut, engineer and USAF officer. He was the Command Module Pilot for the Apollo 15 lunar mission in 1971. He is one of only 24 people to have flown to the Moon and orbited it 74 times in the Command Module Endeavour. In 1982, Worden ran for the United States House of Representatives in Florida's 12th congressional district but lost the Republican primary to Tom Lewis. He was born Jackson, Michigan. Worden died of a stroke on March 18, 2020 in Sugar Land, Texas. He was 88.

Alfredo Enrique Borrero Vega (born 19 October 1955) is an Ecuadorian neurosurgeon and politician. He was the 52nd vice president of Ecuador from 24 May 2021 until 23 November 2023. Borrero Vega was the running mate of Guillermo Lasso and they would win the 2021 election. He is a member of the Creating Opportunities.
Alfred Saunders (12 June 1820 – 28 October 1905) was a New Zealand politician. He was a activist for women's rights in New Zealand. He was born in Wiltshire in England.

Alfred de Vigny (27 March 1797 – 17 September 1863) was a French poet, novelist and playwright. He was born in Loches, France, and died in Paris. He is one of the main writers of French Romanticism, together with Victor Hugo and Alphonse de Lamartine. His best-known works are the historical novel Cinq-Mars (1826), the play Chatterton (1835), the soldier stories Servitude et grandeur militaires (1835), and the eleven poems of Les Destinées, published after his death in 1864. His works often show people who suffer but face their suffering with courage. They also deal with pity, honour, and trust in the human mind. For a long time, people called him "the poet in the ivory tower". This meant that they saw him as a poet who lived apart from public life. The name comes from a playful verse by the critic Sainte-Beuve. Later scholars showed that this picture was too simple. Vigny followed the questions and troubles of his century very closely. Vigny was born on 27 March 1797 in Loches, a small town in Touraine, in central France. His full name was Alfred-Victor de Vigny. His family belonged to the old nobility of the Beauce region. His father, the chevalier (knight) Léon de Vigny, was sixty years old and had been a soldier. Wounds from the Seven Years' War (1756–1763) had left him bent and almost unable to walk. His mother, Marie-Jeanne-Amélie de Baraudin, was about forty years old. Her family had been governors of the royal castle of Loches for a long time. Her father, Didier de Baraudin, had been a squadron commander in the French navy at Brest. Through his mother, Vigny was also related to the explorer Bougainville. Alfred was the fourth son in the family. His three older brothers, Léon, Adolphe, and Emmanuel, had all died when they were small children. Alfred was therefore the only surviving child. He was a weak child, and his parents raised him with great care. His parents had lost money during the French Revolution and had lived through the fear of the Terror. In 1798–1799, the family moved to Paris. Vigny never went back to the town where he was born. His mother taught him herself until he was eight years old. In the evenings, the boy asked his old father many questions about the kings and wars of the past. In 1807, Vigny entered the Hix school near the family home. His school years there were difficult. Other boys treated him badly because he "had a de in his name", which showed that he came from a noble family. In 1811, he moved to the lycée Bonaparte. This was during the years of Napoleon's greatest victories. Paris was filled with the sound of military drums and bells ringing for victories, and pupils shouted "Long live the Emperor!" during their lessons. Although Vigny came from a royalist family, he began, like the other boys, to dream of military glory. His father died in July 1816, when Alfred was nineteen years old. In 1814, Napoleon's Empire fell, and King Louis XVIII returned to France. Vigny was seventeen years old. Because of his family name, he received the rank of second lieutenant in the Gendarmes of the King, one of the "Red Companies" of the royal guard. In March 1815, Napoleon returned from Elba, and the Hundred Days began. The king fled towards Belgium, and Vigny rode with the royal escort as far as Béthune, in northern France. It rained for four days and four nights. Vigny later remembered singing a popular song, Joconde, as loudly as he could. This was the only military campaign in which he took part. A portrait of him from that year, now in the Carnavalet museum, shows a thin young man with fair curly hair. After Waterloo, the Red Companies were disbanded, and in 1816 Vigny joined the foot guards. He then spent quiet years in the garrison towns of Vincennes, Courbevoie, and Rouen. A garrison town is a place where soldiers are stationed in time of peace. His life was filled with military exercises, lessons, parades, and boredom. He became a lieutenant in 1822 and a captain in the 55th line regiment in 1823. That year, France sent an army into Spain. Vigny hoped that he would finally fight, but his regiment only guarded the border in the Pyrenees. From the end of 1824, Vigny lived on leave from the army. On 22 April 1827, his name was removed from the army lists. That day, he wrote in his diary: "italic=no" ("The dream of the glory of arms lasted thirteen years for me"). He added: "I have just ended it with difficulty." Vigny therefore left the army without ever having fought in a battle. Later, his years as a soldier gave him much of the material for Servitude et grandeur militaires. Vigny began writing poetry when he was very young. His two earliest known poems are dated 1815. His first published poem, Le Bal, appeared in December 1820, the same year as Lamartine's Méditations. That same year, he also published his first article, a review of the works of Lord Byron. In March 1822, he published a small book called Poèmes, which contained ten poems. Sadness is already an important part of these early poems. In Paris, Vigny joined the group of young Romantic writers around Victor Hugo. They had their own literary magazine, La Muse française (1823–1824), and met in private homes, where poets read their new poems aloud to one another. Vigny became an important member of the group. He danced well and looked graceful in his military uniform. The writer Mme Ancelot described him as a Don Juan with the charm of a young page. The poet Émile Deschamps wrote that Hugo had shown his greatest strength in the ode, Lamartine in the elegy, and Vigny in the poème, or short narrative poem. Hugo warmly praised Vigny's Éloa in the magazine. La Muse française ended after twelve issues. In July 1824, Vigny told Hugo that he would sincerely mourn the loss of their magazine. At these literary meetings, Vigny fell in love with Delphine Gay, an eighteen-year-old poet. Her mother supported the idea of a marriage, and the poet Marceline Desbordes-Valmore kindly helped the young couple. However, Vigny's mother stopped the plan. Delphine had no fortune and little hope of inheriting one later. Alfred obeyed his mother, but he kept a tender memory of Delphine for the rest of his life. In April 1824, Vigny published Éloa, ou la Sœur des anges ("Eloa, or the Sister of the Angels"). Éloa is a female angel born from a tear of Jesus. She hears about Lucifer, the fallen angel, also called Satan, and feels pity for him. She goes to find him. He speaks to her with gentle but false words. Because of her pure pity, she follows him and falls with him into the darkness. Vigny carried the poem in his mind while his regiment marched from Strasbourg to Bordeaux. Éloa already contains one of the main ideas of his work: pity for every living being that suffers. Moïse ("Moses"), written around 1823, expresses another important idea. Vigny read the Bible closely, but his Moses is different from the Moses of the Bible. He is a great man who is tired of being great. His power and knowledge have separated him from all other people, and he asks God to let him sleep "the sleep of the earth". Vigny later explained the meaning of this figure. He said that Moses represented "the man of genius" in every age. Such a person is alone because his great abilities separate him from other people. These poems were later joined by others in Poèmes antiques et modernes ("Poems Ancient and Modern"), published in 1826. Larger editions followed in 1829 and 1837. The 1829 edition has three parts: poems based on the Bible, poems about ancient Greece, and modern poems. Among the modern poems is Le Cor ("The Horn"), about the death of the hero Roland. In April 1826, Vigny published Cinq-Mars. It was one of the first important French historical novels of the Romantic period. Vigny had loved history since childhood, and he greatly admired Walter Scott. Scott's kind of historical novel was popular in France during the 1820s, and several French writers had already tried to write in this form before Vigny. The story takes place in 1642. The young marquis de Cinq-Mars, a favourite of King Louis XIII, takes part in a plot against Cardinal Richelieu, the king's powerful chief minister. The plot fails, and Cinq-Mars is put to death. In the novel, Richelieu has destroyed the power of the old nobility. By doing this, he has also prepared the way for the later fall of the kings themselves. The critic Pierre-Georges Castex therefore reads the novel as an expression of Vigny's sadness at the decline of his own social class. The novel was a great success. Thirteen editions appeared during Vigny's lifetime. Many readers now saw him as "the French rival of Walter Scott". The biographer Émile Lauvrière calls Cinq-Mars "italic=no", a much-debated work. Vigny freely changed some historical facts, and this brought criticism. However, Louis Maigron, a historian of the historical novel, considered it the first French historical novel of real literary value. Vigny later added a preface called Réflexions sur la vérité dans l'art ("Thoughts on Truth in Art"). In it, he says that an artist may change small historical facts in order to show a more important truth: the ideas and meaning behind the events. While he was in the army near Pau, Vigny fell in love with Lydia Bunbury, the younger daughter of a rich Englishman, Sir Hugh Mills Bunbury. At first, her father refused to allow the marriage. He had little respect for a poor army officer who wrote poetry. In the end, however, he gave his consent. He gave Lydia no dowry. A dowry was money that a father usually gave to his daughter when she married. Vigny and Lydia were married at Pau on 3 February 1825. Lydia never really learned to speak French. Her health was poor from the time of their wedding journey. She lost a baby in 1826 and another in 1829, and the couple never had children. Over time, Lydia became very heavy, and in the end she was almost unable to move. Some visitors even thought that the countess was a housekeeper. Lamartine said that Vigny loved her "like a sick child". For more than thirty years, Vigny described himself as an "eternal sick-nurse". He wrote that caring for a sick person was usually seen as a woman's virtue, and that he was proud to have this quality himself. Money also caused problems. Sir Hugh died in November 1838 and left almost all his property to the children of his second marriage. For six years, Vigny fought the case in the Court of Chancery, an English court known for working very slowly. He travelled to London several times and called the case a torture. In December 1844, Vigny finally accepted an agreement. Lydia would receive a yearly income of 6,500 francs. Around 1827, the Romantic writers became very interested in the theatre. English actors performed plays by Shakespeare in Paris in 1827 and 1828. They gave more than seventy performances, and the young French writers were very excited by them. In 1828, Vigny translated three plays by Shakespeare: Othello, The Merchant of Venice, and, with Émile Deschamps, Romeo and Juliet. Only Othello was ever performed on stage. Vigny's verse translation of Othello, called Le More de Venise (The Moor of Venice), was first performed at the Comédie-Française on 24 October 1829. It broke some of the old rules about the kind of language that could be used in tragedy. The simple word mouchoir ("handkerchief") caused a small scandal because people thought that such an ordinary word did not belong in a serious tragedy. The play was successful and continued to be performed through the winter. Vigny wrote that the reform of theatrical language had now been confirmed by success. A few months later, Hugo's Hernani, first performed in February 1830, won an even greater victory for the same kind of change. Vigny's own historical drama, La Maréchale d'Ancre, was first performed at the Odéon on 25 June 1831. It had only about fifteen performances. A short one-act comedy, Quitte pour la peur, followed in 1833. In July 1830, a revolution forced King Charles X from the throne, and Louis-Philippe became "King of the French". Vigny did not fight for the old royal family. He believed that thirteen years of poorly paid military service had already been enough to pay what he owed to the fallen family. However, Vigny was also critical of the growing power of money under the new government. For a time, he read the works of the social thinkers of his day, including the Saint-Simonians and Lamennais. His poem Paris (1831) presents the city as a place full of new and conflicting ideas. In the poem, there is no clear way to know which ideas to follow. During these years, Vigny began the longest love affair of his life. Marie Dorval was born in 1798 into a poor family of travelling actors. She later became one of the leading actresses of popular drama in Paris. Her acting was natural and full of feeling, very different from the cold classical style. Vigny read La Maréchale d'Ancre at her home in October 1830, and their love affair began in 1831. It lasted for about eight years and was often difficult and full of arguments. At this time, Vigny had to care for two sick people at home: his wife and his mother. Lauvrière explains his new love partly as a way of escaping from this sad home life. Vigny and Dorval had very different characters. He was serious, jealous, and eager to control things. She was free, cheerful, and careless. She sometimes read his letters aloud to her friends, and this hurt him deeply. In 1835, Dorval joined the Comédie-Française. There she first played the role of Kitty Bell in Vigny's Chatterton. Their relationship finally ended in 1838. The following year, the pain of this separation helped to produce Vigny's bitter poem La Colère de Samson. When he heard about Dorval's death in 1849, he was deeply moved. Vigny took the idea for Chatterton from the second story in his book Stello. The play is about the last day in the life of the young English poet Thomas Chatterton, who killed himself in 1770 at the age of seventeen. Vigny wrote the play partly because he wanted to give Marie Dorval an important role. He later reminded her: "Was it a great glory to put on the stage an idea from one of my books? It was for you." The reading committee of the Comédie-Française did not want to accept the play at first. The Duke of Orléans, the king's son, had to intervene before it was accepted. Some actors also worked against Marie Dorval. On the day before the first performance, Vigny was very worried. The first performance took place on 12 February 1835 and was a great success. At midnight, Vigny wrote about his happiness in his diary. He wrote that the success had been greater than even his friends had hoped. The play was performed about forty times in Paris and was then taken to other parts of France. The newspapers gave very different opinions of the play. Le Moniteur criticised what it saw as tiresome praise of suicide, while Le National praised Kitty Bell as a pure and moving character. Many young people were deeply moved by the play and cried during the performances. Other people accused Vigny of making suicide seem attractive to unhappy young men. Vigny answered that he had shown a sickness in society, not given people an example to follow. Vigny's mother had a stroke in 1833, and he cared for her for several years. She died on 21 December 1837. His grief was very deep. Months later, he still saw her in his dreams and sometimes woke with tears on his face. In September 1838, his relationship with Marie Dorval ended. Vigny then went to Maine-Giraud, an old country house in Charente that belonged to his family. There, on 31 October 1838, he finished La Mort du loup (The Death of the Wolf), which he had begun at the end of August. The critic François Germain connects the poem with this time of grief. He says that the silent wolf can be understood as an answer to the death of Vigny's mother. In November, Vigny's father-in-law died, and Vigny travelled to England, where he stayed for about six months. At Shavington, in England, on 7 April 1839, he finished La Colère de Samson. He had begun the poem at Tours in November and had originally called it Dalila. Back in Paris, Vigny continued to live in his flat at 6 rue d'Artois. He had lived there since 1833, and he would later die there. Every Wednesday, he welcomed poets, scholars, and visitors from other countries. The critic Fernand Baldensperger called these meetings "the third Cénacle" of Romanticism. A cénacle was a close group of writers. Baldensperger believed that Vigny's group helped to connect the Romantic poets with the later Symbolists. Vigny also helped the literary world in quieter ways. He gave advice and practical help to writers who were young or poor. The young Provençal poet Joseph Roumanille was one of them. Writers and important visitors from other countries also came to see him. In 1839, Prince Maximilian of Bavaria wrote to Vigny, rather than to the French Academy, and asked him to describe the spirit of French literature. The Danish writer Hans Christian Andersen, famous for his fairy tales, also visited him in Paris. In 1841, Vigny sent the Chamber of Deputies, the lower house of the French parliament, a detailed plan to protect the rights of authors. Vigny wanted to become a member of the French Academy. He tried several times but was not elected. When the Academy voted to replace his friend Charles Nodier, Vigny received three votes, while Mérimée received nineteen. Vigny was finally elected on 8 May 1845. His formal reception into the Academy, on 29 January 1846, went very badly. Before the ceremony, a friend of the government ministers asked him to give up his old royalist views. Vigny politely but firmly refused. Count Molé, who was then director of the Academy, answered Vigny's speech by strongly attacking some of his ideas. He defended Richelieu against the picture of him in Cinq-Mars, and Napoleon against the criticism in Servitude et grandeur militaires. Some people in the hall smiled and clapped during this attack. King Louis-Philippe himself was unhappy about what had happened. He said: "A man honoured in the country should not be received in this way." Vigny was later welcomed at the royal palace. He officially took his seat in the Academy on 2 July 1846, one day after Molé had left his position as director. In February 1848, another revolution made France a republic. Vigny stood for election in Charente. He sent the voters a letter explaining his political ideas. His main rival was a local doctor, who spoke about practical questions such as taxes, railways, and brandy. The country people voted for the doctor. About 76,000 votes were cast, and Vigny received almost none of them. He tried once more in April 1849, without success. He later wrote that living among the peasants had helped him to understand the unhappy state of the country better than ever. From 1848 to 1853, Vigny lived mainly at Maine-Giraud. The estate, with the house and its land, covered about 85 ha. With Philippe, his farm manager, Vigny planted crops, put up new buildings, and made repairs. He grew grapes, and the cognac made from them helped him pay his bills. Vigny wrote in the small tower of the manor. Some people in Paris made fun of the poet who had become a farmer. However, these years in the countryside also produced several of his most important poems. Germain sees a special meaning in the place itself. The manor stands near the centre of an almost perfect circle of hills. He says that this round and closed view suited Vigny's imagination, which was drawn to safe and protective circles. Vigny almost never travelled for pleasure. He never visited Italy. Of Germany he saw no more than a single view across the Rhine from Strasbourg, and he never even saw Lake Geneva. His small income and his duty to care for his sick wife kept him close to home. Vigny accepted the new power of Louis-Napoleon, the future Napoleon III. In January 1852, he welcomed the great public vote, or plebiscite, which he said had defeated "communism". In October 1852, the Prince-President, as Louis-Napoleon was then called, received Vigny at Angoulême and spoke with him for a long time. Vigny again hoped to receive an important public position, but he received none. The Academy, at least, had made him its director for the last months of 1849. Vigny returned to Paris permanently in 1853. Visitors to his home in the rue d’Artois described him as a tall and very polite man with long fair hair. The poet Théodore de Banville also described the quiet flat and Lydia wearing fine lace. In 1857, Vigny helped to carry the funeral cloth at the burial of the poet Alfred de Musset. He continued to write, but very slowly. La Bouteille à la mer appeared in 1854. He added a final stanza to Le Mont des Oliviers about the silence of heaven. The manuscript is dated 2 April 1862, although the editors of the Pléiade edition think that 1863 is more likely. In 1863, he finished his farewell poem, L’Esprit pur. Lydia died on 22 December 1862. Vigny buried her at Montmartre, in the family grave near his mother. He also had his own grave prepared there. Vigny himself was already very ill. He now had attacks of stomach pain every day. The pain was sometimes so strong that he fainted. He had cancer of the stomach. The doctors did not tell him that he had cancer. They said instead that he had a long illness causing stomach pain, which they called gastralgie. He suffered for many months but remained calm, and this deeply impressed his visitors. One of them wrote that Vigny's sense of honour seemed to control "the beauty of his death", just as it had controlled the beauty of his life. He continued to receive friends beside his bed. Baudelaire came and spoke with him for almost three hours. In May 1862, Vigny invited the writer Barbey d’Aurevilly to join a small group of close friends beside what had already become his deathbed. Vigny died in Paris during the night of 16 to 17 September 1863. He had asked for a simple funeral: "Around a coffin one needs only the prayers of the Church and the tears of faithful hearts". His funeral took place on 19 September at his parish church, Saint-Philippe-du-Roule. Only a small number of people were present when he was buried at Montmartre, near his mother and his wife. Twelve days later, Théophile Gautier wrote in Le Moniteur that few writers had ever given such a perfect image of what a poet should be. He also called Éloa perhaps the most perfect poem in the French language. Vigny did not publish much. He revised his writing slowly, and all his poems fit into one small book. However, several of them are among the best-known poems in French literature. The French texts can be read on Wikisource, and links are given in the notes and in the list of main works. Vigny's early collections, from Poèmes (1822) to the final edition of Poèmes antiques et modernes (1837), already show his personal style. Each poem places an idea inside a story or an image. In the preface to the 1837 edition, Vigny explained this method. He said that in each poem "a philosophical thought is presented in an epic or a dramatic form". He also said with pride that he had begun to follow this path "young, but the first". From his early years as a writer, Vigny wanted poetry to be based on the pure music of language. In 1829, he wrote that Voltaire had never understood "italic=no", or "pure poetry". Baldensperger pointed out that Vigny used this expression about a hundred years before the modern debate about pure poetry. Cinq-Mars (1826) made Vigny famous. He defended his freedom to change historical facts in the preface Réflexions sur la vérité dans l'art. He argued that history gives the body of a story, but that art must give it a soul, "the truth of ideas". His picture of Richelieu was sharply criticised. One of the strongest attacks came in Molé's speech at the French Academy in 1846. However, the story moves quickly, and several of its scenes have become famous. This has helped the novel to remain well known. Vigny's works for the theatre include a translation from Shakespeare, Le More de Venise (1829); a dark historical drama, La Maréchale d'Ancre (1831); a short one-act comedy, Quitte pour la peur (1833); and his most successful original play, Chatterton (1835). The editors of the Pléiade edition point out that his whole career in the theatre lasted less than six years. Chatterton is a "drama of thought". One main idea fills its three acts: society kills the poet. Three main characters carry this idea. Chatterton is the poet who refuses to sell his soul. Kitty Bell is the shy young wife who feels pity for him. The old Quaker understands them both. In his famous preface, Dernière nuit de travail (Last Night of Work), Vigny describes three kinds of writers. The first is the man of letters, who writes for a living. The second is the great writer, who helps to guide public opinion. The third is the true poet, a dreamer whom society lets die. Vigny openly asked the state to help young poets who were going hungry. Stello (1832) is not so much a novel as a kind of cure told in the form of a story. Stello is a young poet suffering from deep sadness. He sends for the strange italic=no (Black Doctor). The Doctor tries to cure him by telling three stories about real poets. The first is Nicolas Gilbert, who died in poverty under a king. The second is Thomas Chatterton, who killed himself in England, under a parliament. The third is André Chénier, who was sent to the guillotine during the Revolution. The lesson is harsh: every kind of political power fears and rejects the poet. At the end, the Doctor gives his advice: "to separate the poetic life from the political life". The book was less successful than Cinq-Mars. During Vigny's lifetime, Stello had eight editions, while Cinq-Mars had thirteen. Servitude et grandeur militaires (Military Servitude and Greatness, October 1835) brings together three stories: Laurette ou le Cachet rouge (1833), La Veillée de Vincennes (1834), and La Vie et la mort du capitaine Renaud (1835). They are held together by a frame, that is, a fourth story based on Vigny's own memories as a soldier. In the book, Vigny presents the modern soldier as a kind of slave. He must obey without judging, and blind obedience can turn an honest man into a killer. Joseph de Maistre had argued that war came from God. Vigny rejects this harsh idea and sets against it something entirely human: honour. He wrote in his diary: "italic=no" ("Honour is the poetry of duty"). The critic James Doolittle considered these stories the best of Vigny's prose. He wrote that their plain and natural style is unique in his work, and that soldiers and sailors of every rank speak in their own true language. Les Destinées (The Destinies) brings together Vigny's last ideas about human life and poetry. His friend Louis Ratisbonne, who looked after his papers, published the book in 1864, a few months after Vigny's death. Its full title was Les Destinées, poèmes philosophiques (The Destinies, Philosophical Poems). The book contains eleven poems. Seven had already been printed, in the Revue des Deux Mondes between 1843 and 1854 or in the months around Vigny's death. The other four appeared for the first time in the book. It is not certain which of the two titles, Les Destinées or Poèmes philosophiques, Vigny finally wanted, because he had used both. Baldensperger doubted that Vigny's final choice could ever be known. Lauvrière thought that Ratisbonne probably followed Vigny's spoken wishes, both for the title and for the order of the poems. The Pléiade editors, who studied all the papers, add that the title had disappeared for a time but returned during Vigny's last period of work. They also say that the eleven poems follow a planned order. Les Destinées stands at the beginning, L'Esprit pur gives the final answer, and La Mort du loup comes at the exact centre. The opening poem, Les Destinées, was finished at Maine-Giraud on 27 August 1849, a few months after Vigny's second defeat in an election. It is written in terza rima, the linked three-line stanzas used by Dante. The poem asks whether Christ has freed human beings from blind fate. Its answer is dark: grace has only taken the old name of destiny. Germain reads this fate above all as something inside the mind, born from the fears of childhood. La Maison du berger (The Shepherd's Hut, 1844) is a long poem about love and thought. The poet asks a woman he loves, Éva, to leave the cities and travel with him in a shepherd's hut on wheels. Nature is beautiful but cold, and gives no answer. Only the human heart can share our feelings. For Germain, Éva is the answer to all the dreams of Stello, who stands for the poet's inner self. One line gives the main idea of all Vigny's work: J'aime la majesté des souffrances humaines. (I love the majesty of human suffering.) Vigny noted: "This line is the meaning of all my philosophical poems." La Mort du loup (The Death of the Wolf, published 1843) tells the story of a hunt at night. An old wolf is trapped. He fights in silence and dies without a sound. The hunter understands the lesson: Gémir, pleurer, prier est également lâche. [...] Puis, après, comme moi, souffre et meurs sans parler. (To moan, to weep, to pray is equally cowardly. [...] Then, like me, suffer and die without a word.) Le Mont des Oliviers (The Mount of Olives, written in 1839 and published in 1843) shows Jesus alone at night on the Mount of Olives, before his death. He asks his Father why evil exists, but heaven remains silent. During his last years, Vigny added a final stanza called Le Silence. Since heaven says nothing, the just man will meet this absence with a cold and proud silence of his own. Le Juste opposera le dédain à l'absence. (The just man will answer absence with disdain.) La Colère de Samson (The Anger of Samson, written in 1839) turns Vigny's break with Marie Dorval into a story from the Bible: Samson is betrayed by Delilah. The wounded lover curses what he sees as the endless conflict between man and woman. La Sauvage (The Savage Woman, 1843) defends law, home, and settled work against wild freedom. La Flûte (The Flute, 1843) shows pity for people whose weak powers cannot reach their own dreams. Les Oracles passes judgement on the politicians who talked a great deal during the last years of the fallen monarchy. Wanda tells the true story of a Russian princess who chose to follow her condemned husband to Siberia. Vigny blames the tsar above all for refusing to give her children a book from which they could learn to read. Ten years later, after the Crimean War, he added lines that present the fall of Sevastopol as a punishment from above. La Bouteille à la mer (The Bottle in the Sea) gives an answer to despair. "A book is a bottle thrown into the open sea", Vigny had written in 1842. He finished the poem on 27 September 1847, except for the opening stanza, which he added in 1853. The poem appeared only in 1854. A young sea captain is overcome by a storm. He puts his notes and maps into a bottle, closes it, and throws it into the waves. With this bottle, the poet says, the captain has defeated Death. Sooner or later, the bottle will reach a port. The young reader of the poem, a new Stello, even hears the advice: "Forget Chatterton". The final line expresses Vigny's belief: Le vrai Dieu, le Dieu fort, est le Dieu des idées. (The true God, the strong God, is the God of ideas.) L'Esprit pur (The Pure Spirit) was planned over almost twenty years and finished in the spring of 1863, a few months before Vigny's death. It closes the book with a final message to Éva. His noble ancestors, who were hunters and soldiers, left behind only a name. Vigny, the last of his line, leaves a written work. Through writing, he enters the only kingdom that lasts. The final line calls the Pure Spirit "king of the world". Daphné, written around 1837 and first published in 1912, was planned as a second meeting with the Docteur Noir. Its hero is the Roman emperor Julian, who tried to bring back the old gods. Through Julian, Vigny asks what happens to people when a religion dies. Another unfinished novel, L’Alméh (1831), was set in Egypt. Throughout his life, Vigny kept notebooks in which he wrote down his thoughts. Ratisbonne published a selection from them in 1867 as Le Journal d’un poète (A Poet’s Diary). The modern Pléiade edition of 1948 gave a much fuller text. Many of Vigny's most famous sentences come from these notebooks. Pessimism is the belief that pain and evil hold a large place in human life. Vigny accepted this idea with open eyes. In his work, heaven is silent: people suffer and pray, but they receive no answer. Georges Bonnefoy says that in the years when he was writing Stello, Vigny's work was marked by a "sceptical Christ", a Christ who doubts. However, Vigny never stopped studying religions. The list of books that he borrowed from the Royal Library fills several pages in Bonnefoy's study. For Bonnefoy, Vigny's religious thought is above all "a defence of man". Vigny gives two answers to the silence of heaven. The first is pity. From Éloa, with its angel born from a tear, to his last poems, the same idea returns: if God seems absent, human beings must love and help one another. The second answer is quiet courage. Vigny's stoicism, the old idea of facing pain without complaining, is not simply a harsh kind of pride. Lauvrière calls it a "softened stoicism", made warmer by pity. The wolf in La Mort du loup gives the rule: do your long task, then suffer and die without a word. When religious faith disappears, one light remains for Vigny: honour. Honour asks for nothing from heaven. It is the respect that a person has for himself. For Vigny, it is the soldier's human religion, "the poetry of duty". Bonnefoy showed that honour is also the principle that the italic=no was looking for when he tried to help the unhappy Stello: good judgement for the mind and greatness for the heart. Germain describes the same idea from another angle. Honour is like armour built around a frightened heart. Vigny himself called it "italic=no" ("an iron circle made of will and pride"). However, Vigny's pessimism does not end in despair. For him, ideas can live longer than people. In La Maison du berger, poetry is described as a "diamond" whose light must travel far. Germain follows this image throughout Vigny's work. The diamond is a hard and clear stone that protects deep thoughts against time. In La Bouteille à la mer, the bottle in the sea carries the knowledge of a dead man towards unknown people in the future. Vigny's final poems therefore create what Castex calls a "religion of the Spirit": a faith in the written thought of humanity. For Vigny, the poet is an outsider whom society rejects. Every kind of political power uses the poet, fears him, and may leave him to die in poverty. However, the poet is also the true maker of the laws of the future. Vigny took neither of the two main paths of other writers of his time. He did not choose direct political action, as Hugo and Lamartine did, and he did not choose art for art's sake, as Gautier did. Vigny wrote little and worked very slowly. In his notebooks, he kept single lines that he called "verses to make". Some of these lines waited for years before he found the right poem for them. He usually kept to traditional French verse forms, especially the alexandrine, the twelve-syllable French line. Inside this old form, however, he placed new subjects: modern doubt, modern suffering, and modern hope. His main method is the symbol. He does not simply explain an idea. Instead, he gives the idea a story or an image. As he said himself, he presents thought "in an epic or a dramatic form": a wolf, a bottle, or a shepherd's hut on wheels. Doolittle notes that one main idea stands behind each of Vigny's mature works. The story and the symbol give this idea a visible form. Germain studied Vigny's images in great detail. He explains that clear symbols teach the reader, while darker symbols help the poet to discover his own thoughts. Even colours form a system. Black and red are connected with fear and blood, while gold and the light of the diamond suggest happiness and hope. Some lines in Vigny's poems stand alone almost like proverbs. Critics call them his verse-maxims. His gift for writing short, strong, memorable statements is one reason why his poetry is often quoted. His prose has two main styles. His early novels use rich and decorative language. In Servitude et grandeur militaires, his prose becomes much simpler and more natural. Doolittle says that this style stands apart in Vigny's work and has kept its strength. In his own lifetime, Vigny stood in the shadow of Victor Hugo. His fame grew after his death, in several stages that Baldensperger studied in detail. The Parnassian poets, and later the Symbolists, learned from his use of ideas and symbols. His Wednesday meetings had also formed a living bridge between different generations of poets. In the 20th century, newly found papers were published by Baldensperger, Henri Guillemin, Jean Sangnier, and others. These documents changed the old picture of Vigny as a cold and distant man. They showed instead a man deeply troubled by the great questions of his time. In 1962, François Germain studied Vigny's inner world image by image. Doolittle calls Germain's book the most detailed study of Vigny as a writer. Writing in 1967, Doolittle went even further. He argued that among the French poets between André Chénier and Baudelaire, Vigny should be placed highest, above Hugo, Lamartine, and Musset. He saw Vigny as an early guide for modern poets and writers, from Baudelaire and Mallarmé to Saint-Exupéry and Camus. The silent wolf, the bottle floating on the sea, and the angel born from a tear are among the best-known images in Vigny's poetry. Dates are those of first publication.
