Adams is divorced and has two children. She is noted for the many different hats that she wears.

Almazbek Sharshenovich Atambayev (, Almazbek Şarşenoviç (Şarşen uulu) Atambayev; born 17 September 1956) is a Kyrgyz politician. He was the President of Kyrgyzstan from 1 December 2011 to 24 November 2017. He was Prime Minister of Kyrgyzstan from 17 December 2010 to 1 December 2011 and from 29 March 2007 to 28 November 2007.

Alma G. Stallworth (November 15, 1932 – August 25, 2020) was an American Democratic politician and businesswoman. She was in the Michigan House of Representatives from 1971 to 1974, 1983 to 1996 and from 2003 to 2004. She also founded the Black Caucus Foundation of Michigan in 1985. Stallworth was born in Little Rock, Arkansas. Stallworth died on August 25, 2020 in Detroit, Michigan at the age of 87.

Alois Philipp Maria, Hereditary Prince of Liechtenstein and Regent of Liechtenstein, Count of Rietberg (born 11 June 1968), is the first in line to the throne of Liechtenstein. He is the eldest son of Hans Adam II, Prince of Liechtenstein, and Countess Marie Aglaë Kinsky of Wchinitz and Tettau. Alois has been regent of Liechtenstein (Stellvertreter des Fürsten) since 15 August 2004. As such, he has undertaken many royal duties on behalf of his father. He is married to Duchess Sophie of Bavaria. 11 June 1968 - 13 November 1989: His Serene Highness Prince Alois of Liechtenstein, Count of Rietberg 13 November 1989 - present His Serene Highness The Hereditary Prince of Liechtenstein, Count of Rietberg 15 August 2004: His Serene Highness The Regent of Liechtenstein

Alois Brunner (8 April 1912 – c. 2010) was an Austrian Schutzstaffel (SS) officer. Brunner was wanted for war crimes, and was Adolf Eichmann's assistant. Eichmann referred to Brunner as his "best man". Brunner was wanted for sending at least 140,000 European Jews to the gas chambers. He was commander of the Drancy internment camp outside Paris from June 1943 to August 1944, from which nearly 24,000 people were deported. He was sentenced to death in absentia in France in 1954 for crimes against humanity. In 1961 and in 1980, Brunner lost an eye and the fingers of his left hand, as a result of letter bombs sent to him by the Israeli intelligence service, called Mossad. In 2003, the Guardian described him as "the world's highest-ranking Nazi fugitive believed still alive". Brunner was last reported to be living in Syria, whose government had long refused international efforts to locate or apprehend him. There were rumours that he would be extradited, however, after the Syrian Civil War broke out it became hard to negotiate any kind of settlement with the Assad regime, which controlled Syria during Brunner's stay. Other sources suggest he died already in December 2001. He was sentenced again, now to life imprisonment, in France the same year. It has been determined that Brunner helped the Syrian government develop chemical weapons which were later allegedly used on rebels.

Alois Mock (10 June 1934 – 1 June 2017) was a politician. He was a member of the Austrian People's Party (ÖVP). He was Vice Chancellor of Austria from 1987 to 1989. As foreign minister, from 1987 through 1995, he helped take Austria into the European Union. Mock died on 1 June 2017 from complications of Parkinson's disease at the age of 82.

Alonso de Ercilla y Zúñiga (August 7, 1533–November 29, 1594), was a Spanish nobleman, soldier and epic poet. While in Chile (1556–63) he fought against the Araucanian Indians, and there he began the epic poem La Araucana, said to be the greatest Spanish historical poem. This heroic work in 37 cantos is divided into three parts, published in 1569, 1578, and 1589. It tells of the brave uprising of the Araucanians and also tells the history of Chile and of contemporary Spain.

Alon Carl Wieland (April 26, 1935 – January 22, 2022) was an American Republican politician and businessman. He was a member of the North Dakota House of Representatives, from 2002 to 2014. He was the Commissioner of Cass County, North Dakota from 1983 to 2003. Wieland was born in Underwood, North Dakota. Wieland died in West Fargo, North Dakota on January 22, 2022, at the age of 86.

Sir Alok Sharma (born 7 September 1967) is a British politician. He was the President of COP27 from 2021 to 2022. He was formerly the Minister of State at the Cabinet Office from 8 January 2021 to 25 October 2022 and President for COP26 from 8 January 2021 to 6 November 2022. Resigning from his previous role as Secretary of State for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy to lead COP26, he retains a full Cabinet position. Sharma was a Conservative MP for Reading West from 2010 to 2024.

Saint Aloysius Gonzaga (9 March 1568 - 21 June 1591) was born in the family's castle of Castiglione delle Stiviere in Italy and died at 23 while in training to be a Jesuit. He is a saint in the Roman Catholic Church. In 1576, at the age of eight, he was sent to Florence with his brother at the court of the Duke of Florence. After leaving Florence he met St. Charles Borromeo and from him received First Communion. After a period at the court in Spain he returned to Italy and he renounced his heritage in favor of his brother. Though in delicate health, he cared for those suffering from an epidemic in Rome, hence his early death. He was beatified in 1605 and made saint in 1726. The feast day is celebrated on June 21.

Aloïse Moudileno Massengo (11 March 1933 – 6 January 2020) was a Congolese politician and lawyer. He served as Vice President of the Republic of the Congo from 1971 to 1972. He has been called the first Congolese lawyer. He was born in Vindza District. Moudileno Massengo died on 6 January 2020 in the French city of Nancy. He was 86.

Aloyzas Sakalas (6 July 1931 – 18 July 2022) was a Lithuanian physicist and politician. He was known as one of the signers of the Act of the Re-Establishment of the State of Lithuania. He was a Member of the European Parliament with the Social Democratic Party of Lithuania from 2004 to 2009. Before, he was a member of the Seimas from 1990 to 2004. He was born in Anykščiai, Lithuania. Sakalas died on 18 July 2022, two weeks after his 91st birthday in Vilnius, Lithuania.

Alpha Condé (born 4 March 1938) is a Guinean politician. He became the President of Guinea. He began his term as President in 2010. The president before him was Sékouba Konaté. The news reported he may have been bribed by a mining company. Condé was arrested and removed from power on 5 September 2021 by members of the Republic of Guinea Armed Forces. On December 9, 2022, the US Treasury published a list of more than forty personalities targeted by sanctions for acts of corruption and human rights violations. Among the targets of the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC), the financial control body of the Treasury Department is Alpha Condé..

Alpha Oumar Konaré (born 2 February 1946) is a former President of Mali for two five-year terms (1992 to 2002), and was Chairperson of the African Union Commission from 2003 to 2008. In September 2021, Konaré was urgently hospitalized in Morocco at Cheikh Zaid Hospital in Rabat.

Alphonse of Poitiers or Alfonso or Alphonse (11 November 1220 – 21 August 1271) was the Count of Poitou from 1225 and Count of Toulouse (as Alfonso II) from 1247. Alphonse was a son of Louis VIII, King of France and Blanche of Castile. He was a younger brother of Louis IX of France and an older brother of Charles I of Sicily. The Treaty of Paris stipulated that a brother of King Louis was to marry Joan of Toulouse, daughter of Raymond VII of Toulouse, and so in 1237 Alphonse married her. Honest and moderate, protecting the middle classes against exactions of the nobles, he exercised a happy influence upon the south, in spite of his naturally despotic character and his continual and pressing need of money. He is noted for ordering the first recorded local expulsion of Jews, when he did so in Poitou in 1249. Aside from the crusades, Alfonso stayed primarily in Paris, governing his estates by officials, inspectors who reviewed the officials work, and a constant stream of messages. When Louis IX again engaged in a crusade (the Eighth Crusade), Alphonse again raised a large sum of money and accompanied his brother. This time, however, he did not return to France, dying while on his way back, probably at Savona in Italy, on 21 August 1271.

Alphonso Taft (November 5, 1810 – May 21, 1891) was the United States Attorney General and United States Secretary of War under President Ulysses S. Grant. He was the father of U.S. President and Chief Justice William Howard Taft. Taft was born on November 15, 1810 in Townshend, Vermont. He was raised in Cincinnati, Ohio. Taft stuided at Yale College, at Yale Law School, and at Yale University. He was married to Fanny Phelps from 1841 until her death in 1951. They had five children. Then he was married to Lousie Maria Torrey from 1853 until his death in 1891. They had five children. Taft died on May 21, 1891 in San Diego, California from heart failure, aged 80.

Alphons Egli (8 October 1924 – 5 August 2016) was a Swiss politician. He was a member of the Swiss Federal Council (1983–1986). He was elected to the Federal Council of Switzerland on 8 December 1982 and handed over office on 31 December 1986. He had connections to the Christian Democratic People's Party of Switzerland. He was also President of the Confederation in 1986. Egli was a citizen of Entlebuch and Lucerne.

Alpin II was a king of Dalriada and the father of Kenneth & Donald MacAlpin, his name was Aílpin mac Echdach in Gaelic, he ruled as king of Dalriada in 834 and some even say he was king of Scots although his son was the first to be king of Scots in 843/848. He was born in 778 and died July 20th 834 fighting the Picts in Galloway, after his death Kenneth MacAlpin became king of Dalriada but many others claimed the throne and he also become king of Pictland with the same happening there. He was buried later in July 834 in Galloway.

Alphonso R. Jackson (born September 9, 1945) is an American Republican politician. He was the 13th United States Secretary of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) from 2004 to 2008. He was nominated by President George W. Bush.

Alphonsus Gerardus Martinus "Alphons" Panis (25 January 1900 – 22 February 1975) was a Dutch politician. Panis was the son of teacher Leonardus Waltherus Panis (1852-1933) and Anna Maria Cornelia van Roessel (1857-1914). He grew up in a large Catholic family. Several brothers became priests, including the titular bishop Walther Panis; one sister joined the Sisters of St. Francis. His brother Constant Panis became a known architect in Tilburg. Panis worked at the municipal clerk of Berkel-Enschot. In 1926 he started working as a secretary at the municipality of Helvoirt. In 1929, Panis was appointed mayor of Berkel-Enschot. Eight years later in 1937 he was appointed mayor of Haaren. In 1947 he returned to the municipality of Berkel-Enschot to become mayor there again. Panis retired in 1965. His son Fons Panis (1932 – 2023) was mayor of Maartensdijk (1973-1978) and mayor of Leusden (1987-1997). He died in 1975 at the age of 75.

Alphonse Poaty-Souchlaty (25 March 1941 – 24 October 2024) was a Congolese politician. He was the Prime Minister of Congo-Brazzaville from 7 August 1989 to 3 December 1990 under President Denis Sassou Nguesso. Poaty-Souchlaty died on 24 October 2024, at the age of 83.

Alphonse de Lamartine (21 October 1790 – 28 February 1869) was a French poet, writer, and politician. His full name was Alphonse Marie Louis de Prat de Lamartine. He is remembered for two very different reasons. First, he changed French poetry. In March 1820, he published a small book of twenty-four poems called Méditations poétiques ("Poetic Meditations"). The book made him famous in only a few weeks. The year 1820 is often used to mark the beginning of French Romanticism in poetry. However, Marius-François Guyard, who edited the poems, warns that this date is mainly a useful way of dividing literary history. Lamartine continued to use much of the language and many of the verse forms of the previous century. What was new was mainly his personal voice, not his poetic technique. Second, Lamartine was for a short time the leading figure in the government of France. In February 1848, the king lost his throne. Lamartine became minister of foreign affairs in the provisional government. He was never the official head of state, but in practice he was the man who led the government. For about three months, he was the best-known man in France. He spoke to angry crowds in the streets and was able to calm them. However, he soon lost almost all his support. In the election for president in December 1848, he received 17,940 votes out of more than seven million. This was about one vote in every four hundred. Lamartine also wrote history books, travel books, and novels. His Histoire des Girondins (1847) was a very popular history of the French Revolution. In parliament, he spoke against slavery and the death penalty. He also supported schools for poor children, savings banks, and railways. Lamartine spent much more money than he earned. During his last years, he wrote page after page only to pay his debts. He even had to sell the house where he had spent his childhood. He died deeply in debt and with much less political power than he had possessed in 1848. However, he had not been forgotten. Two years before his death, parliament had voted to give him a national payment, and his death was followed by public tributes. His grave is at Saint-Point in Burgundy. The earliest ancestor known to historians was Benoît Jean. He was a tanner and shoemaker in Cluny, in Burgundy, around 1550. His children became traders in the same town. Some of their descendants worked for the monks of the great abbey of Cluny, while others became Protestants. In 1651 Étienne Alamartine bought a government office called "secretary to the king". By buying this office, he became noble and received the right to use a coat of arms. The family later wrote its name as "de La Martine" and then as "de Lamartine". The Lamartines were therefore noble, but they did not belong to one of the great or powerful noble families. Their nobility was fairly recent. Alphonse himself showed little interest in proving that his family was old or important. The poet's father was Pierre de Lamartine, known as the chevalier de Pratz. He was the youngest of three sons. By family custom, the eldest son was expected to keep the main estates. The second son entered the Church, while Pierre entered the army. Younger sons in such families often remained single. Pierre's eldest brother decided not to marry, and his second brother remained a priest. The family line was therefore in danger of ending. Pierre was at last allowed to marry. He was about thirty-eight years old. He married Françoise-Alix des Roys, who had been born in Lyon on 8 November 1766. Her father, Jean-Louis des Roys, managed the estates of the duke of Orléans. Her mother, Marie-Marguerite Gravault, was an assistant governess to the duke's children. As a little girl, Alix played with the boy who later became King Louis Philippe. Her education was also watched over by Madame de Genlis, the chief governess of the Orléans children. Alix grew up in an educated household. Among the well-known people who visited her mother's drawing room were d'Alembert, Buffon, Laclos, Gibbon and Rousseau. Alix read Rousseau and Bernardin de Saint-Pierre closely, and this education later shaped the lessons that she gave her son. The marriage contract was signed in Lyon on 4 January 1790. The wedding took place three days later, on 7 January, in the church of Ainay. The couple did not have a great fortune, but they were not poor. Pierre received the right to live on and use the small family estate of Milly, near Mâcon. At first, he did not own the estate itself. Milly covered about fifty-two hectares. A little more than one third of the land was planted with vines and fruit trees. The rest was woodland and grassland. About ten farm workers were needed to work the estate, which gave the family an income of about 12,000 francs a year. Alix brought furniture, family jewels and 50,000 francs into the marriage. However, one third of this money could not be given to her until the death of an uncle. Alphonse was not his parents' only child. His younger brother, Félix, died as a young child, and a sister named Clémentine, born in 1797, died before she was one year old. Alphonse grew up with five sisters as the only surviving boy. His father's two brothers and three sisters had no children. They followed the old family custom of keeping the land together, even after the Revolution had ended the legal right of the eldest son to receive almost everything. They therefore treated Alphonse as the future heir to much of the family property. In return, he had to make a yearly payment to each of his five sisters. As a young man, Lamartine believed that these lands would one day make him very rich. He did not understand how many costs and family payments came with them. This false idea of his future wealth encouraged him to spend and borrow too much, and it helped to cause his serious money problems later in life. Lamartine was born on 21 October 1790 in Mâcon, in a small house in the rue des Ursulines. It stood next to the larger house owned by his family. For a long time, many readers thought that he had been born at Milly. This belief came partly from his poem Milly ou la terre natale ("Milly, or the Land Where I Was Born"). Milly was not his birthplace. It was a village that he loved and where he spent an important part of his childhood. In later life, Lamartine often reshaped his past when he wrote about it. His Confidences, his Mémoires and his later comments on his poems mix fact, memory and literary invention. Historians therefore compare them with his letters, his mother's journal and official records. Lamartine's family belonged to the small country nobility. It was strongly Catholic and loyal to the king. In May 1792 his father went to Paris and offered his sword to Louis XVI. On 10 August he helped to defend the Tuileries Palace. He was wounded and arrested during the fighting, but he escaped with the help of a gardener and returned to the area around Mâcon. The French Revolution was less violent in the Mâcon area than it was in Paris or Lyon. Pierre de Lamartine did not leave France. In October 1793 the revolutionary authorities arrested him again. He remained in the former convent of the Ursulines at Mâcon until October 1794. His wife and children were kept under watch in the small family house. Lamartine later said that his earliest memories were of his father in prison, his mother alone in a guarded house, revolutionary songs in the streets and the sound of the guillotine in the public square. These were memories written down many years after the events. After the Terror, the family spent more time at Milly. Alphonse played with the village children, learned to ride at an early age and kept his love of horses and dogs throughout his life. He saw the work of the vineyard closely and knew the smells of the wine cellar and the stable. This direct knowledge of country life later appeared in many of his poems and stories. The sources do not give the same date for the family's move to Milly. Bertrand, following Lamartine's own memories, places it when the boy was about four or five. Guyard's chronology says that the family settled there in the autumn of 1797, when he was seven. During these years they generally stayed at Milly in summer and autumn and returned to Mâcon for the winter. His father bought the old and partly ruined château of Saint-Point around 1800. In 1805 the family also moved into a larger house in Mâcon, the hôtel d'Ozenay. Lamartine later liked to describe himself as a poor country boy. This picture was not fully true. He had been born in a town, and his family, although it did not have a large income, was noble and owned land. In 1848 this picture of a country childhood helped him present himself as a man close to ordinary people in the countryside. His mother, Françoise-Alix des Roys, had a strong influence on his early education. She gave him his first lessons and wanted him to become a faithful Catholic. In spite of what Lamartine later suggested in the Confidences, his childhood education was firmly Catholic. He wrote that, when he looked at his mother, God seemed to stand behind her. From 1800 she kept a private journal in which she wrote about her thoughts, her religious life and events within the family. After her death, Lamartine prepared parts of it for publication under the title Le Manuscrit de ma mère ("My Mother's Manuscript"). The published book is not a true copy of the journal. Some pages of the original were cut or damaged, and some passages in the book were written or changed by Lamartine himself. Lamartine first received lessons at the village school and from the abbé Dumont, the priest of the nearby village of Bussières. Dumont's earlier life had been unusual. He had managed the lands of the comte de Pierreclau, and he had a son with one of the count's daughters, Jacqueline-Marguerite, who was known in the area as Mademoiselle de Milly. Her family sent her away and later arranged her marriage to a banker in Lyon. During the Revolution, Dumont served in local government and later returned to church work. His neighbours did not always know what he truly believed. Lamartine's mother knew about his reputation but still trusted him with the education of her only son. This story later became one of the sources for Lamartine's long poem Jocelyn. Dumont helped him create the priest Jocelyn, while Jacqueline-Marguerite helped him create Laurence, the young woman whom the priest cannot marry. The sources disagree about Dumont's religious life. Toesca says that he took the oath required by the revolutionary state and began saying Mass again in 1801. Montplaisir, following research by Pierre de Lacretelle, says that Dumont did not become a priest until 1798. On 2 March 1801 Lamartine entered the Puppier boarding school in Lyon. He was very unhappy there. On 9 December 1802 he ran away, but the police found him and brought him back. He remained at the school until the end of the school year. On 27 October 1803 he entered the school of the Fathers of the Faith at Belley, close to Savoy. He was much happier there. The teachers treated their pupils with kindness and spoke to their feelings as well as to their memory. He remained at Belley until the end of January 1808 and left because of poor health. At Belley he studied Greek and Latin writers and French classical authors such as Boileau and Racine. One of his teachers also introduced him to the work of Chateaubriand. His wider reading began mainly after he left the school. Between 1808 and 1810 he read works by Alexander Pope, Laurence Sterne and Ossian. He also read many French writers of the eighteenth century, including Voltaire and Parny, but Jean-Jacques Rousseau had the greatest influence on him. La Nouvelle Héloïse ("The New Heloise") moved him deeply. In letters to a friend, he wrote that he wanted to love like Rousseau's hero Saint-Preux and, above all, to write like Rousseau. These early readings helped to shape his ideas about love, nature and poetry. When Lamartine left the school at Belley in January 1808, he had no clear idea of his future. His strongly royalist family did not want him to enter the service of Napoleon. His father and grandfather had served in the royal army, and the family regarded Napoleon as a man who had taken the throne and whose wars were using up the young men of France. In January 1809 Lamartine went to Lyon. He attended concerts and plays, visited libraries, began to gamble and made his first debts. He said that he would study law, but he did not yet follow a regular course. In March 1809 his number was drawn for forced military service. His family paid for another man to take his place, as the law allowed, but Lamartine was then called to serve in person as well. His father used his good relations with government officials to have him declared unfit because of poor health. At the right moment, Lamartine began to spit blood and could eat only chicken and vegetable broth. When the danger had passed, his health quickly improved. He returned to Milly in September 1809. From January to May 1810 he lived in Lyon again and was meant to study law. He soon stopped going to most of his lessons. He spent his time at theatres, gaming tables and meetings with friends, and again made debts. During these years he moved between Milly, Mâcon, Lyon and the homes of friends and relations. He read a great deal, wrote poems and had several short love affairs. He wanted a place in public service or diplomacy, but he did not want to tie himself closely to Napoleon's government. In March 1811 he became a member of the Academy of Mâcon and gave a talk about foreign literature. In July 1811 his family agreed that he should travel to Italy with Monsieur and Madame Haste, who were going there on business and for their wedding trip. Lamartine travelled through Chambéry, Turin and Milan before reaching Livorno in August. He then went on alone to Rome and arrived in Naples at the end of November 1811. Guyard's chronology gives 1 December as the date of his arrival. In Naples he knew Antoine Dareste de La Chavanne, a family connection who was the director of the royal tobacco factory. Lamartine first chose to live at an inn because he did not want anyone to watch him. When he ran short of money, he accepted Dareste's offer and moved into his home in the first days of January 1812. There he began a love affair with a young working woman. She was paid as a worker at the tobacco factory and also helped in Dareste's household. Later research identified her as Antoniella Giacomino, whose family name is also written Iacomino. Lamartine and his friend Aymon de Virieu left Naples in early April 1812, probably on 6 April. Some older accounts place the departure in March, but Guyard's chronology and later research place it in April. Lamartine returned to Mâcon on 5 May. The young woman's identity caused confusion for more than a century. In his different accounts, Lamartine seemed to describe two women: an older woman called Antoniella and a younger one called Graziella. Early biographers therefore believed that they were two different people. Whitehouse, writing in 1918, thought that Antoniella was Dareste's housekeeper and that she watched over the younger girl. In 1942 the marquis de Luppé showed that Antoniella and Graziella were two names for the same person. In 1963 Abel Verdier found Antoniella Giacomino in the parish records and established more details of her true history. She died young, probably from tuberculosis. Dareste told Lamartine of her death in the spring of 1816. The news led him to write or rewrite four poems in her memory: À Elvire, Le Golfe de Baya, près de Naples, À El*** and Tristesse. The first two later appeared in the Méditations poétiques, and the other two in the Nouvelles Méditations poétiques. Elvire was a poetic name and was not the young woman's real name. Lamartine later used it for more than one woman. More than thirty years after the journey, while staying on the island of Ischia in 1844, Lamartine turned the memory into a longer story. He called the young woman Graziella, a form of the Italian name Grazia. In the story she is the daughter of a poor fisherman from Procida. She refuses a marriage arranged by her family because she loves the young French visitor. After he leaves Italy, she dies of grief. The story first appeared as part of Les Confidences in 1849. It was published as a separate book under the title Graziella in 1852. Lamartine changed the dates, the places, the ages and many events. The book is therefore a work of literature based on a real memory, not a reliable account of what happened. An old report says that Lamartine later told Émile Ollivier that people blamed him for Graziella's death even though she had not died and had become the mother of many children. Whitehouse repeated this story from an earlier study. It is only a report made long after the event, and the later research into Antoniella's life does not support it. The memory of Antoniella remained in Lamartine's work. Agide Pirazzini found signs of it in the later stories Geneviève, Le Tailleur de pierres de Saint-Point, Fior d'Aliza and Antoniella, and in the poem La Fille du pêcheur of 1857. Pirazzini also argued that some lines in Le Crucifix, a poem connected mainly with Julie Charles, may have come from Lamartine's memory of the young woman of Naples. This is a critical interpretation, not a fact that can be proved. After his return to France, Lamartine still had no settled career. In May 1812 he became the unpaid mayor of Milly. This office gave him something to do and also protected him from a new call for military service. His main public work was to protect the village well and add a rope and pulley so that people could raise the bucket more safely. He continued to gamble and to make debts. He also read a satire about gambling to the Academy of Mâcon. In August 1812 he planned an epic poem called Clovis and wrote a first version of the tragedy Saül. He later worked on other tragedies, including Médée and Zoraïde. These works still followed the style of the French classical theatre. During this period he had a relationship with Anne-Josèphe, called Nina, the separated wife of his friend, the chevalier de Pierreclau. She lived at the castle of Cormatin with her father, Pierre Dezoteux, baron de Cormatin. He was a former officer who had fought in the American Revolutionary War. Nina had foreign contacts. Through her, Lamartine received books by English Romantic poets in their original language, although Napoleon's Continental Blockade made such books difficult to obtain in France. These readings added to his knowledge of English poetry, but his own poems at this time still followed older French forms. Nina gave birth to Léon de Pierreclau at Cormatin on 1 March 1813. Her husband was the boy's legal father, but Guyard, Toesca and most later biographers regard Lamartine as his biological father. Lamartine never publicly gave Léon his name. Whitehouse, writing in 1918, said that the fatherhood was often suspected but not proved and did not decide the question. Lamartine later watched closely over Léon's education and treated him as his ward. Their letters show a close relationship. On 28 March 1838 Léon married Alix de Cessiat, one of Lamartine's nieces. In 1814 the armies fighting Napoleon entered France, and the Bourbons returned to power. Lamartine hoped for a place in diplomacy or local government, but none was offered to him. Instead, he entered the military household of Louis XVIII as a garde du corps, or member of the king's bodyguard. He reported for service in Paris on 10 July 1814. Later that month he was sent to Beauvais, where he trained on foot and on horseback. At the end of August he returned to Paris and guarded the king at the Tuileries Palace. In November he received leave and returned to Milly. On 1 March 1815 Napoleon returned from Elba, beginning the period known as the Hundred Days. Lamartine was ordered to return to his unit. He joined the royal household and followed the king's forces north from Paris. At Béthune the king's bodyguard was released from service because Louis XVIII and the royal family were leaving France. Lamartine chose not to follow them abroad. He returned secretly to Paris and then went back to Burgundy. As he would not serve Napoleon and feared another call for military service, he later crossed the border into Switzerland. He stayed near Nyon and then spent part of June at Nernier, on the Savoy side of Lake Geneva. After Napoleon's defeat at Waterloo and the second return of Louis XVIII, Lamartine went back to the king's bodyguard. His name appears again in its records on 1 August 1815. He spent a short time at Beauvais and then served in Paris. He disliked military life and resigned on 1 November 1815. Lamartine was now twenty-five years old. He still had no settled profession and depended on his family while carrying heavy debts. He was known in a few local literary circles, but he had not published a book. Some poems written during these years, including Adieu in 1815, were later revised and included in the Méditations poétiques. In 1816 Lamartine was in poor health and suffered from pains in his liver. One doctor advised him to go to Vichy, while another recommended Aix-les-Bains, in Savoy. He chose Aix and left Mâcon on 30 September 1816. After spending a few days with his friend Louis de Vignet at Chambéry, he reached Aix at the beginning of October. Aix was then a small town of fewer than 2,000 people. It was known for its warm springs and received about 800 visitors each year. Lamartine stayed in the modest guest house of Doctor Perrier. The building was more like a country inn than a large hotel, and it was almost empty after the end of the summer season. A young woman from Paris had arrived at the same house about two weeks before him. Her name was Julie Charles. She had been born Julie-Françoise Bouchaud des Hérettes in Paris on 4 July 1784 and was six years older than Lamartine. Her family had strong links with the French colony of Saint-Domingue, which is now Haiti. Her mother's family owned land there and lost much of its wealth during the Haitian Revolution. The exact story of Julie's childhood is uncertain. Lamartine later wrote that her mother drowned while trying to escape from the island and that Julie was saved from the sea. Whitehouse says that the surviving records do not support this romantic story. La Fournière goes further and thinks that Julie probably never lived in the Caribbean. The biographers therefore do not agree about these early years. What is certain is that Julie lost her mother while she was young and that her family suffered serious money problems. She spent part of her childhood with relations in France and knew periods of poverty before entering the educated society of Paris. In 1804 she married Jacques-Alexandre Charles, a famous scientist who was thirty-eight years older than her. In 1783 he had made one of the first human flights in a balloon filled with hydrogen. A law about gases still carries his name. He was a leading member of the Academy of Sciences and librarian of the Institut. The couple lived in an official flat inside the Institut building. Julie held a salon in this flat. Writers, scientists, government officials and royalist politicians met there. She was intelligent, well educated and able to help young people by introducing them to important members of Paris society. By 1816 Julie was seriously ill. Doctors called her illness "phthisis", a wasting disease of the lungs that was probably tuberculosis. Her health had become worse during the year, and she had been sent to take the waters and breathe the mountain air. Lamartine arrived at the Perrier guest house on about 6 October 1816. Julie usually ate in her room and went outside only for short walks in the garden. They probably first met under the vines in the garden of the house. In Raphaël, the story that he wrote many years later, Lamartine said that a storm on the lake brought them together. Julie's small boat was said to have been caught by the wind, and Lamartine came to save her. Biographers think that he greatly changed or enlarged this event. There may have been a sudden wind that forced both boats towards the same part of the shore, but it is not possible to know exactly what happened. The important fact is that they quickly fell in love. During the following three weeks they walked beside the lake and through the nearby hills. They visited Tresserve, Hautecombe, Grésy and the Charmettes, the house connected with Jean-Jacques Rousseau. Julie was thirty-two, Lamartine was twenty-five, and both were in poor health. Their relationship was not only an exchange of ideas and feelings. A letter that Lamartine wrote to Virieu in December 1816 says clearly that they had been lovers. Near the end of their stay, however, they decided to end the physical part of their relationship. The surviving letters suggest that this change came mainly from Lamartine. He described their new bond as a pure and spiritual friendship, or as the bond between a son and a mother. On 26 October Lamartine and Julie left Aix together with Vignet. After visiting the Charmettes, they travelled as far as Mâcon, where they parted. They then began a long and passionate correspondence. In January 1817 Lamartine went to Paris. He remained there until May and often saw Julie, either in her flat at the Institut or during walks in the parks around Paris. She introduced him to her husband, who received him kindly, and she worked hard to help him find a government position. Through her salon he met the minister of the interior, Joseph-Henri Lainé; the baron Mounier; and the count of Rayneval, an official in the foreign ministry. He also met the ultra-royalist writer Louis de Bonald. These meetings gave the young man from Burgundy his first entry into leading political and literary circles in Paris. Julie also encouraged his writing. She asked Virieu to bring her copies of his poems and urged Lamartine to begin work again on his tragedy Saül. She told Virieu that Lamartine's happiness, future and fame had become the centre of her own life. After leaving Paris, Lamartine returned to Burgundy. His health was still poor, and he first went to Vichy. As the treatment did not help him, he returned to Aix in the middle of August 1817. He hoped that Julie would join him there, as they had planned. Her illness had become much worse, however, and she could no longer travel. Lamartine waited for her beside the lake of Bourget during August and September. He visited the places where they had walked together in the previous year. Alone and unhappy, he wrote Le Lac ("The Lake"), which became his best-known poem. In the poem the poet returns alone to a place where he had once been happy with the woman he loves. He asks time to stop and asks the lake, the rocks, the wind and the trees to keep the memory of their love. Its most famous line asks time to hold back its flight. Lamartine wrote the poem while Julie was still alive. He knew that her illness was serious, but he did not know that she would die so soon. After her death, readers naturally understood the poem as a song of mourning. This later knowledge changed the way in which the poem was read. During the autumn Julie's health became much worse. On 10 November 1817 she wrote that she had received the last rites. Her illness had brought her back towards the Catholic faith, and Lamartine and some of her friends had encouraged her to make peace with the Church. Lamartine wanted to return to Paris and see her. He could not do so because he had no money left and could no longer borrow. Julie Charles died in Paris on 18 December 1817, after several months of suffering. Lamartine learned of her death at Milly on 25 December. In a letter to Virieu, he wrote that he was deeply unhappy but found some comfort in the thought that Julie was no longer suffering. Very little of their correspondence survives. After Julie's death, Lamartine burned the letters that she had sent him. He also asked Virieu to recover the letters that he had written to her. Four letters from Julie were later found at Saint-Point by René Doumic. They show that her love for Lamartine was real and strong. Lamartine never forgot her. In 1865 he told his secretary Dargaud that she was the woman whom he had loved most. In his poems he did not use Julie's real name. He called her Elvire, but he had already used this name for Antoniella, the young woman whom he had known in Naples. The name came from older French poetry, especially the poems of Parny, and did not belong to one woman alone. Guyard explains that Elvire is not a true portrait of Julie. She is the figure of the loved and lost woman. Other women, including Lamartine's wife Marianne and his niece Valentine, may have inspired as many poems as Julie did. His poetry also came from family love, friendship and the deaths of people close to him. Julie Charles did not give Lamartine his poetic gift, but the meeting helped him find the voice that later made him famous. Without this love and loss, he might have continued writing correct but ordinary poems in the older style for much longer. During 1818 and 1819 Lamartine made several visits to Paris. His poems were already known in some literary and political salons before they appeared in a book. Two of his friends played an important part in making them known. The first was Aymon de Virieu, his closest friend from the school at Belley. Virieu helped copies of the poems pass from one reader to another and spoke in their favour. Lamartine had great trust in his judgement. He often sent him new poems and rarely thought that a poem was finished before Virieu had read it. The second was Eugène de Genoude, a young writer who was then preparing a French translation of the Bible. Lamartine later said that he had read some of the Psalms and the Prophets in his mother's prayer books, but had never read the Bible closely or in order. Genoude sometimes came to his room in the morning with the proofs of his translation. Their readings helped Lamartine discover new images and a higher form of religious poetry. They directly inspired La Poésie sacrée. Genoude also helped Lamartine find a bookseller. The volume was printed by the Didot press and sold at number 12 in the rue de Seine, at the depot of the Greek, Latin and German bookshop run by Henri Nicolle. The title page names neither Lamartine nor Nicolle. Nicolle's nephew Charles Gosselin later took over the business and published the following editions. Lamartine had hesitated for a long time before publishing his poems. In April 1819 the duke of Rohan had two or three of them privately printed by Didot in about twenty copies. Seeing his verse in print encouraged Lamartine, while the poems continued to pass from hand to hand in Paris. By the end of 1819 he had stronger reasons to publish. He had large debts and needed money. He also hoped that success as a writer would help him obtain a diplomatic position. Such a position would in turn make it easier for him to marry Marianne Birch, whose mother did not wish her daughter to marry a man without a career or an income. In January 1820 Lamartine became seriously ill with a disease of the lungs, usually described by his biographers as pneumonia. His mother came to Paris to care for him. Thinking that he might die, he asked for a priest and made a general confession. He recovered slowly and came out of the illness with a stronger attachment to the Catholic faith. The Méditations poétiques went on sale on 11 March 1820. Whitehouse and some older sources give 13 March, but Guyard's critical edition and chronology give 11 March. The first printing contained only 500 copies. The volume was a thin book of 118 pages and carried no author's name. This did not keep Lamartine's identity secret. Most of the poems had already been copied, read aloud or discussed in the Paris salons. Genoude carefully prepared for the arrival of the book. From 4 March he sent a notice, sample pages and favourable information to important newspapers. He also wrote an article about the book for Le Conservateur. This use of the press helped the poems reach readers outside the salons. The first 500 copies sold out in about ten days. A second edition of 1,500 copies appeared at the beginning of April. It carried Lamartine's name and added two poems, La Retraite and Le Génie. Some later biographers give a different list, but these are the two additions named in Guyard's critical study of the early editions. New editions followed quickly: six had appeared by the autumn of 1820, and a ninth, dated 1823, went on sale at the end of December 1822. Between 1820 and 1831 nineteen editions were issued by Nicolle's business and then by Gosselin. There were also copies printed without permission in Belgium and elsewhere. Gustave Lanson estimated that between 35,000 and 40,000 copies were sold during the first ten years. These figures are estimates, but they show that the success was unusually large for a book of poems. The royal government welcomed the book. Louis XVIII praised the poems, and the minister of the interior sent Lamartine fine editions of French and Latin classical writers. The king later granted him a pension to add to his small diplomatic income. On 27 March 1820 Lamartine was appointed second attaché, a junior post at the French legation in Naples. His literary success had helped him enter the diplomatic service. Talleyrand was also said to have read the poems until four in the morning. The story comes partly from Lamartine's later memories, but letters sent at the time show that Talleyrand warmly praised the volume. The eighteen-year-old Victor Hugo reviewed the book in the Conservateur littéraire on 15 April 1820. He compared Lamartine with André Chénier and saw him as a writer who joined classical form to the new Romantic spirit. He welcomed the book as the work of a true poet and encouraged its author to continue. The newspapers paid most attention to the religious and philosophical poems. The wider public preferred the poems of loneliness, lost love and memory. Women were especially moved by them. The countess Dash later remembered that many young women wished to become an Elvire and went out at night to look at the moon beside lakes and under trees. Some older critics disliked the poems. They thought that Lamartine complained too much and did not follow the clear language expected in classical verse. The academician François Andrieux laughed at the weak and dying poet who appeared in several pieces. Such attacks did not stop the success of the book. Lamartine later wrote that the jokes of the critics had passed away, while his verses had remained in the hearts of young people and women. This was written long after the event, but it describes the difference between the first reviews and the response of ordinary readers. The first edition contained twenty-four poems. They were written at different times between about 1815 and 1820. They do not tell a continuous story and are not placed in the order in which they were written. Guyard therefore does not see a strict plan in the collection. However, the book begins with loneliness and ends with sacred poetry, which gives it a broad movement from sadness and doubt towards religious hope. L'Isolement ("Loneliness") opens the book. The poet sits on a mountain under an old oak at sunset. He sees the river, the lake, the mountains and the evening star, but the beauty of the world no longer gives him pleasure because the person he loves is absent. The poem contains Lamartine's best-known line: one person is missing, and the whole world seems empty. The poem brings together many of the subjects found later in the book: solitude, memory, mountains, lakes, the evening sky, lost happiness and the hope of another life. For this reason Toesca compares it to the opening of an opera, where the main musical ideas can already be heard. Le Vallon ("The Valley") presents a peaceful place where the tired heart hopes to find rest. L'Automne ("Autumn"), the twenty-third poem of the first edition, looks at the beauty of nature at the moment when both the year and human life seem close to their end. Le Lac, written beside the lake of Bourget in 1817, is the tenth poem in the first edition and stands near the centre of the collection. La Prière ("The Prayer") is the twelfth poem. It shows all of nature joining in an act of worship. The universe becomes a temple, the earth an altar, the sky its roof and the stars its lights. Lamartine later said that he valued this poem very highly. Le Désespoir ("Despair"), the sixth poem, speaks against a God who allows suffering. It was begun in July 1818 and finished in November. La Providence à l'homme ("Providence speaks to man"), which follows it, gives God's answer. Lamartine completed this reply in May 1819. He admitted that he wrote it unwillingly because he thought that Le Désespoir could not enter the book without an answer. The two poems should therefore be read together. Le Chrétien mourant ("The Dying Christian") was connected with Lamartine's serious illness at the beginning of 1820. Its calm acceptance of death reflects the religious change that he experienced during his recovery. La Poésie sacrée ("Sacred Poetry") is the twenty-fourth and final poem. It was inspired by Lamartine's readings with Genoude. The poet passes through scenes from the Bible and then tells his lyre and the voices of the prophets to become silent before the coming of Christ. The Méditations did not make a complete break with older French poetry. Lamartine continued to use regular rhyme, twelve-syllable lines, familiar verse forms and much of the noble language of the eighteenth century. Many of his images came from earlier writers such as Parny, Léonard, Rousseau and Chateaubriand. The book could therefore seem new without appearing strange or difficult to its first readers. What was new was mainly the voice. Readers felt that a living person was speaking directly about his sadness, his love, his doubts and his hope in God. The poems did not give the exact facts of Lamartine's life, but they turned private feelings into experiences that many readers could share. Nature also received a new place in the poems. Lamartine did not usually try to give a clear and exact picture of a lake, a valley or a night sky. The landscape carries the feeling of the person who looks at it. The outer world and the state of the soul seem to become one. Sainte-Beuve first objected to Lamartine's words "melancholy lakes". He thought that a more exact description, such as "blue lakes", would be better. He later changed his mind. He understood that the word "melancholy" did not describe the colour of the water but joined the landscape to the poet's feeling. He then wrote that no blue lake was worth Lamartine's line. The collection also joined love and religion. Readers influenced by Rousseau could respond to its personal feeling and its love of nature. Readers of Chateaubriand could recognise its Christian language and its search for faith. Yet the book also contains doubt, anger and uncertainty. Its deepest unity comes from a soul that has not yet found complete peace. The year 1820 is often used as the beginning of French Romantic poetry. This date is useful, but it must not hide Lamartine's strong links with the eighteenth century. His verse forms were not revolutionary. What changed French poetry was the personal voice, the music of the lines and the way in which feeling entered the landscape. Lamartine later explained the success by saying that readers had heard a soul and seen a human being rather than only a book.

Alson Sherman (April 21, 1811 – September 27, 1903) was an American politician from Chicago who was the Mayor of Chicago from 1844 through 1845. Sherman was married to April 21, 1811 in Barre, Vermont. He was married to Aurora Abbott from 1833 until her death in 1883. They had 14 children. Sherman died on September 27, 1903 in Waukegan, Illinois, aged 92.

Altaf Gauhar or sometimes written Altaf Gohar (1923-2000) was a Pakistani civil servant, journalist and writer. He is best known for having helped to write the biography of the notorious Pakistani military dictator General.Ayub Khan.

Altamas Kabir (19 July 1948 – 19 February 2017) was an Indian lawyer and judge. He served as the 39th Chief Justice to the Supreme Court of India from 29 September 2012 through 18 July 2013. He was born and raised in Kolkata, West Bengal. Kabir died of kidney disease in Kolkata on 19 February 2017, aged 68.

Altero Matteoli (8 September 1940 – 18 December 2017) was an Italian politician. He was born in Cecina, Tuscany. Matteoli was a member of Forza Italia party. He served as a member of Senate of the Republic. From June 2001 to May 2006, he was the Minister of Environment. He served as Minister of Infrastructures and Transport from May 2008 to November 2011. He was also the mayor of Orbetello from 29 May 2006 to 16 May 2011. Matteoli died in a car accident on 18 December 2017 in Capalbio, Tuscany at the age of 77.

Alton Gold Keel Jr. (born September 15, 1943) is an American engineer, diplomat, and businessman. He was born in Hampton, Virginia. In July 1986, President Ronald Reagan appointed Keel as the acting principal deputy to the National Security Advisor. From 1987-89, Keel was the United States Permanent Representative to NATO.

Alun Michael born August 22, 1943, is a Welsh politician. He graduated from Keele University. He was the First Minister of Wales. He also was the first Minister of the National Assembly for Wales. He was a journalist for the South Wales Echo from 1966 to 1971.

Alun Arthur Gwynne Jones, Baron Chalfont, (5 December 1919 – 10 January 2020) was a British politician. He was a retired British Army officer and historian. He was awarded the Efficiency Medal in October 1950. He was a minister in the Foreign and Commonwealth Office from 1964 to 1970 and appointed to the Privy Council in the former year. On 27 March 1967, in the House of Lords, Chalfont became the spokesman/figurehead for Harold Wilson. He was the author of several military history books on subjects including the Napoleonic Wars. He retired from the House of Lords on 10 November 2015. Jones died on 10 January 2020 at the age of 100.

Alveda Celeste King (born January 22, 1951) is an American conservative activist, author, and former state representative for the 28th District in the Georgia House of Representatives. She is a niece of civil rights leader Martin Luther King Jr. and daughter of civil rights activist A. D. King and his wife, Naomi Barber King. She is a Fox News Channel contributor. She once served as a senior fellow at the Alexis de Tocqueville Institution, a conservative Washington, D.C., think tank. She is a former member of the Georgia House of Representatives and the founder of Alveda King Ministries.

Alvard Petrossyan (, October 4, 1946 – March 10, 2022) was an Armenian writer, philologist, publicist and politician. She was born in Yerevan, Armenia. She was a deputy in the National Assembly for the Armenian Revolutionary Federation from 1999 until 2012. Petrossyan died on March 10, 2022 in Yerevan at the age of 75.

Alvey Augustus Adee (November 27, 1842 – July 4, 1924) was an American politicians and diplomat. He was a long-time official with the United States Department of State. He served as the acting Secretary of State in 1898 during the Spanish-American War.

Alvin James Baldus (April 27, 1926 – February 2, 2017) was an American politician. He was member of the Democratic Party. He served in the United States House of Representatives from 1975 to 1981, as a member for Wisconsin. He lost his re-election in 1980. Baldus was born in Garner, Iowa. He grew up in Elkton and Austin in Minnesota. He studied at Riverland Community College. Baldus died on February 2, 2017 in Menomonie, Wisconsin, aged 90.

Alvin Elliot Roth (born December 18, 1951) is an American academic. He is the Craig and Susan McCaw professor of economics at Stanford University and the Gund professor of economics and business administration emeritus at Harvard University. He was President of the American Economics Association in 2017. In 2012, he was awarded the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences alongside Lloyd Shapley for their contributions to the theory of stable allocations and the development of practical market design.

Alvin Adolf Holmes (October 26, 1939 – November 21, 2020) was an American politician. He was a member of the Alabama House of Representatives from 1974 to 2018. He was a member of the Democratic Party. He was born in Montgomery, Alabama. Holmes died on November 21, 2020, at the age of 81.

Alvin Leonard Bragg Jr. (born October 21, 1973) is an American politician, attorney and the current New York County District Attorney since 2022. In 2021, Bragg became the first African American elected to the office. He had previously served as chief deputy attorney general of New York and as an assistant United States attorney in the Southern District of New York.

Alyson Judith Kirtley Bailes CMG (6 April 1949 – 29 April 2016) was an English diplomat, political scientist, academic and polyglot. She served as the British Ambassador to Finland from November 2000 to June 2002. She was born in Liverpool. Bailed died on 29 April 2016 of pancreatic cancer in Glasgow, Scotland, aged 67.

Aly Mahmoud Lotfy (6 October 1935 – 27 May 2018) was an Egyptian politician. He served as Prime Minister of Egypt from 4 September 1985 to 9 November 1986 during the Hosni Mubarak presidency. He was born in Al-Adwa, Faiyum, Egypt. He was a member of the National Democratic Party. Mahmoud died on 27 May 2018 in Cairo at the age of 82.

Alwin Brück (23 September 1931 – 14 February 2020) was a German politician. He was a member of the Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD). He was Parliamentary Secretary of the Federal Ministry of Economic Cooperation and Development from 1974 to 1982. He also was Deputy of the Bundestag from 1965 to 1969 and Substitute Member of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe from 1969 to 1970. Brück was born in Heusweiler, Germany. Brück died on 14 February 2020 at the age of 88.

Alí Rodríguez Araque (9 September 1937 – 19 November 2018) was a Venezuelan politician, lawyer, and diplomat. He was born in Ejido, Mérida, Venezuela. He was the leader of the party Patria Para Todos. He worked under the Hugo Chávez administration, such as oil advisor, General Secretary of OPEC, President of Petróleos de Venezuela (PDVSA), Minister of External Relations and Ambassador to Cuba. He was appointed as Minister of Finance in June 2008. His last occupation was Ambassador of Venezuela from 2014 until his death in 2018. Rodríguez Araque died on 19 November 2018 in Havana, Cuba from a heart attack at the age of 81.

Alércio Dias (22 December 1942 – 3 September 2020) was a Brazilian lawyer and politician. Dias was born in Joinville, Santa Catarina. He was a member of the Chamber of Deputies between 1983 to 1991, representing Acre for the Democratic Social Party. He was also a member of the Acre Legislative Assembly between 1995 to 1999. Dias died on 3 September 2020 in Rio Branco, Acre from problems caused by a gastrointestinal hemorrhage, aged 77.

General (ret) Amadou Toumani Touré (November 4, 1948 – November 10, 2020) was the president of Mali. He took power from a military ruler, Moussa Traoré in 1991, then he gave power to civilian (non-military) authorities in 1992. He won the presidential election in 2002. He won the next election easily in 2007. He was born in Mopti, Mali. Touré died on November 10, 2020 in Istanbul, Turkey just one week after his 72nd birthday.

Amado Boudou (born November 19, 1963) is an Argentine businessman. He was the 35th Vice President of Argentina from December 2011 through December 2015. Before he was Minister of the Economy from 2009 to 2011. In 2012 he was accused of influence peddling and money laundering. He was sentenced to five years and ten months in prison, and banned for life from holding public office.

Amadou Soumahoro (31 October 1953 – 7 May 2022) was an Ivorian politician. He was in the National Assembly constituency of Séguéla from 2011 until his death and was President of the National Assembly from 7 March 2019 until his death. He also the President of the Assemblée parlementaire de la Francophonie from 9 July 2019 until his death. Soumahoro was born in Séguéla, Ivory Coast. Soumahoro died on 7 May 2022 in Abidjan, Ivory Coast at the age of 68.

Amadou Cheiffou (born 1942) is a Nigerien politician. He served the State as Head of Government from October 27, 1991 to April 17, 1993. Cheiffou ran as a candidate for the Democratic Social Rally party (RSD-Gaskiya) in the presidential elections called on November 16, 2004, and was fourth of six candidates by winning 6.35% of the votes. Cheiffou graduated from the French Civil Aviation University.

Amadou Ba (born 17 May 1961) is a Senegalese politician who served as Prime Minister of Senegal from 17 September 2022 to 6 March 2024. He unsuccessfully ran for President of Senegal in 2024. He also was the Foreign Minister of Senegal from 2019 to 2020. He was Minister of Finance and Economy from 2013–2019. Ba was listed as one of the Top 100 most influential Africans by New African magazine in 2011, 2012 and 2013.

Amalasuntha (c. 495 – 30 April 534/535) was a queen of the Ostrogoths, a branch of Goths, from 526 to 534. She was a Gothic princess and daughter of the Italian king, Theodoric the Great. Amalasuntha had been married to Eutharic, an unknown Gothic nobleman. She gave birth to a son named Athalaric in 518. Her husband later died, leaving Amalasuntha a widow to raise their young son. After her son Athalaric died, she fought for the kingdom, which was very difficult, but it increased her support of the Romans. Amalasuntha was an extremely well educated woman. She studied Greek and Latin and she became a lifelong contributor of writings and arts. Theodoric (her father) supplied her with a Roman education because he had an interest in creating peaceful Roman-Gothic relations. Her husband Eutharic was assigned Theodoric's heir, which excluded Theodoric's nephew from inheritance and power. Her husband Eutharic died in 522, and Theodoric followed in 526. As a result, Athalaric inherited the throne. Athalaric was still very young so Amalasuntha became the regent Her accomplishments over her years of being a regent, were applauded by many people like the historian Procopius who spoke of her bravery and knowledge. She pursued her goal of creating good connections between the Romans and the Goths, which had been torn down in the years of her father’s rule, mostly during the imprisonment of Theodoric and the killing of Boethius, a Roman political figure. She gave Boethius back his captured estates and began to look for the Roman Senate and then sent a letter to the emperor of Constantinople, asking him to forgive her and gave a Roman education to her son. All of this to get on the emperors good side. Amalasuntha attempted to improve relations with barbarian people to make peace with the Gothic nobility. Amalasuntha improved relations with the Burgundians, but the alliance ended.

Amal Nasser el-Din (; 31 July 1928 – 9 February 2025) was an Israeli Druze writer and politician. He served as a member of the Knesset for Likud between 1977 and 1988. Nasser el-Din was born in Daliyat al-Karmel, Mandatory Palestine. Din died on 9 February 2025, at the age of 96.

Amal Clooney (née Alamuddin;; born 3 February 1978) is a Lebanese lawyer. Her works focused in international law and human rights. She was born in Beirut to Lebanese Druze parents. Her clients include Julian Assange, the founder of WikiLeaks, the former prime minister of Ukraine, Yulia Tymoshenko; Canadian journalist Mohamed Fahmy; and Nobel Prize laureate Nadia Murad. In 2019, Clooney was appointed the special envoy on media freedom by the British Foreign and Commonwealth Office. In September 2021, The International Criminal Court (ICC) appointed Amal Clooney, as Special Advisor for the Sudanese conflict in Darfur.
Aman Mikael Andom (1924-1974) was an Eritrean general who was made Chairman of the Derg, and was Head of State of Ethiopia from 15 September until 17 November, 1974.

Aman Lal Modi (born 21 September, 1985) is a Nepalese politician and social worker who represents Morang 4 in the House of Representatives. He was also a member of the 2nd Nepalese Constituent Assembly, having been elected from the Unified CPN (Maoist) party.

Amalric (; 113611 July 1174), formerly known as Amalric I, was the king of Jerusalem from 1163 until his death. His Muslim enemies called him the bravest and cleverest of the crusader kings. Amalric was the younger son of King Fulk and Queen Melisende. His elder brother, King Baldwin III, was their mother's co-ruler.

Amanda Anne Milling (born 12 March 1975) is a British Conservative Party politician. She was the Chairwoman of the Conservative Party alongside Ben Elliot and Minister without Portfolio from February 2020 to September 2022. Milling was the Member of Parliament (MP) for Cannock Chase from 2015 general election until 2024.

Amanda Jane Solloway (née Edghill; born 6 June 1961) is a British Conservative Party politician. She was a Member of Parliament (MP) for Derby North from 2019 to 2024. She also was Science Minister from 2019 to 2024.

Amanda S. C. Gorman (born in Los Angeles on March 7, 1998) is an American poet, writer, speaker, and political activist. She read one of her poems during the installment ceremony of the American President Joe Biden in January 2021. She was the first person to become National Youth Poet Laureate. She became the first poet to perform (a poem) at a Super Bowl; She delivered (or read out) her poem "Chorus of the Captains" at Super Bowl 55.

Amanda Sofia Margareta Lind (; born 2 August 1980) is a Swedish politician and psychologist. She has been the co-spokesperson of the Green Party since 2024. Between 2019 and 2021, she was the Minister for Culture and Democracy in the second Löfven cabinet.

Amanullah Khan (24 August 1934 – 26 April 2016) was a Pakistani activist and writer. He was born in Astore. He was the founding leader of the Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front. It was a pro-independence militant activist group in the former state of Jammu and Kashmir. He was the co-founder of the Kashmir Independent Committee in 1963. He was elected Secretary General of JK Plebiscite Front (PF) in 1965. He Co-founded the JK National Liberation Front (NLF) with Maqbool Bhat. Khan died on 26 April 2016 at a hospital from chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in Rawalpindi, Pakistan, aged 82.

Amar Singh (27 January 1956 – 1 August 2020) was an Indian politician. He was one of the leaders of the Samajwadi Party. He was a member of the Rajya Sabha from 2016 until his death. On August 1, 2020, at the age of 64, Singh died from kidney failure at a hospital in Singapore.

Amar Singh I, the Maharana ruler of Mewar Kingdom (16 March 1559 – 26 January 1620), was the eldest son and successor of Maharana Pratap I. He was the 14th Rana of Mewar, ruling from 19 January 1597 until his death on 26 January 1620.
Amanibakhi was a Kushite King of Meroe. His reign dates to the 4th century BCE. Amanibakhi was the successor of Akhraten and the predecessor of Nastasen. The burial place of Amanibakhi is not known.

Amaro Silva (c. 1957 – March 27, 2015) was a Canadian politician. He was born in Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada. He served on the Winnipeg City Council from 1992 to 1998. Silva died on March 27, 2015 following a "serious illness", aged 57.

Amata Kabua (November 17, 1928 – 20 December 1996) was a Marshallese politician. He was the first President of the Marshall Islands from 1979 to 1996. Kabua died in office after a long illness, on December 20, 1996, in Honolulu, Hawaii, aged 68.

Amath Dansokho (January 13, 1937 – August 23, 2019) was a Senegalese politician. He was Secretary-General of the Party of Independence and Work (PIT) for years. He was Minister of Urban Planning and Housing from 1991 to 1995 and again in 2000. He was mayor of Kédougou from 2005 through 2012.

Amarinder Singh (born 11 March 1942) is an Indian politician, military historian, former royal and former veteran. He was the 15th Chief Minister of Punjab. He was a Member of the Legislative Assembly from Patiala. In 1980, he won a seat in the Lok Sabha for the first time. Singh resigned as the Chief Minister of Punjab on 18 September 2021.

Amaru Topa Inca, also known as Amaru Inca Yupanqui, was an Inca prince and co-ruler of the Hanan dynasty, who reigned around 1450. He was the son of Pachacuti and Mama Anawarki. Around 1450, Pachacuti decided to name him his co-ruler and successor. His reign lasted between five and ten years.

Amata Catherine Coleman Radewagen (; born December 29, 1947), commonly known as Aumua Amata, is an American Samoan politician. She has been the delegate for the United States House of Representatives from American Samoa since 2015. Radewagen is a member of the Republican Party. Amata is the first woman to represent American Samoa in the U.S. Congress.

Amber Rudd (born 1 August 1963) is a British Conservative Party politician who served as Member of Parliament (MP) for the East Sussex constituency of Hastings and Rye from 2010 to 2019 and was Home Secretary between July 2016 and April 2018. Her appointment as Home Secretary made her the fifth woman to hold one of the Great Offices of State. In 2018 Rudd resigned as Home Secretary following the Windrush scandal and was replaced by Sajid Javid. She returned to government as Secretary of State for Work and Pensions in November 2018.

Ambrose Everett Burnside (May 23, 1824 – September 13, 1881) was an American soldier, railroad executive and politician. He served as governor of Rhode Island (1866-1869) and U.S. Senator from Rhode Island. As a Union Army general in the American Civil War, he fought successful campaigns in North Carolina and East Tennessee but was defeated in the disastrous Battle of Fredericksburg and Battle of the Crater. Burnside commanded the IX Corps, the Department of Ohio, and also the Army of the Potomac for a few months. His distinctive style of facial hair is now known as sideburns, derived from his last name.

Sir Ambrose Dundas Flux Dundas KCIE, CSI (b.1899-d.1973) was the second chief commissioner of Balochistan (Pakistan) from 4 October 1947 - 8 April 1948, and the second governor of the North West Frontier Province from 9 April 1948 - 16 July 1949. Dundas was Lieutenant Governor of the Isle of Man from 1952 to 1959.

Ambrose Mandvulo Dlamini (5 March 1968 – 13 December 2020) was a Swazi business executive and politician. He was the tenth Prime Minister of Eswatini from October 2018 until his death in December 2020. He was the CEO of Swazi MTN. On October 27, 2018, King Mswati III announced in a gathering at the royal kraal at Lobamba that Dlamini would be the country’s next Prime Minister. Dlamini tested positive for COVID-19 on 15 November 2020 and was hospitalized eight days later after developing mild symptoms. He died at a hospital in South Africa on 13 December at the age of 52. According to the Constitution of Eswatini, Masuku will serve as acting prime minister for a maximum period of three months.

Makhdoom Muhammad Ameen Faheem (; alt. spelling: Amin Fahim; 4 August 1939 – 21 November 2015), was an Pakistani populist left-wing figure and a poet and Spiritual leader, He was the senior vice-chairman of Pakistan Peoples Party. He was also the chairman of Pakistan People's Party Parliamentarians and former chairman of Alliance for Restoration of Democracy. He served as the Commerce Minister of Pakistan serving from 3 November 2008 through 16 March 2013. born on August 4, 1939 in Hala Sindh, Pakistan, was the eldest son of Makhdoom Muhammad Zaman, Faheem died on 21 November 2015 from leukemia after being admitted to a hospital in Karachi, Pakistan under ICU at the age of 76.
Dr. Bibi Ameenah Firdaus Gurib-Fakim GCSK (born 17 October 1959) is a Mauritian politician and biodiversity scientist. She was the 6th President of Mauritius from 2015 to 2018.

Ameena Begum, also known as Dr. Ameena Shafiq, is a Bangladeshis politician and former member of parliament. She was a member of the Jatiya Sangshad from 2001 to 2006, from women's reserved seat-31 (national 331) for the Bangladesh Jamaat-e-Islami.

Maulana Ameer Zaman (; 1956 – 7 September 2021) was a Pakistani politician. He was Minister for Postal Services from August 2017 to May 2018. He had been a member of the National Assembly of Pakistan, from June 2013 to May 2018. Zaman died on 7 September 2021 at the age of 65.

Amelia Platts Boynton Robinson (August 18, 1911 – August 26, 2015) was an American activist. She was a leader of the Civil Rights Movement in Selma, Alabama and a key figure in the 1965 march that became known as Bloody Sunday. In 1984 she became founding vice-president of the Schiller Institute working with Lyndon LaRouche. She was awarded the Martin Luther King, Jr. Freedom Medal in 1990. Robinson died in Montgomery, Alabama after suffering a series of strokes at the age of 104.

Amelita "Ming" Jara Martinez-Ramos (born December 29, 1926) is the wife of Fidel V. Ramos–the twelfth President of the Philippines–and was the eleventh First Lady of the Philippines from 1992 to 1998.

Ameurfina Aguinaldo Melencio-Herrera (11 May 1922 – 12 October 2020) was a Filipino judge. She served as an Associate Justice of the Philippine Supreme Court from 1979 until her retirement in 1992. She was the second woman appointed to the Supreme Court, filling the vacancy left by the retirement of the first female Supreme Court Justice, Cecilia Muñoz-Palma. Melencio-Herrera died in Cabanatuan on 12 October 2020, aged 98.

Ameya Pawar (born April 22, 1980) is an American politician. He was the alderman for the 47th Ward of the City of Chicago. He was first elected in the 2011 municipal elections, and was elected to a second term on February 24, 2015. Pawar's 2015 re-election was secured with over 82% of the vote, the largest margin in the election cycle. Pawar is the first Indian American and Asian American in Chicago City Council history. He was a candidate in the Democratic Party primary for Governor of Illinois in the 2018 election. He lost the primary to businessman JB Pritzker.
Amerish Babulal "Ami" Bera (; born March 2, 1965) is an American doctor and politician who in 2013 became a member of the United States House of Representatives from California.
Amine Pierre Gemayel (; born 22 January 1942) is a Lebanese politician. He was the President of Lebanon from 1982 to 1988 and was the leader of Kataeb Party.
Amina Jane Mohammed (born 27 June 1961) is a Nigerian politician. She is the fifth Deputy Secretary-General of the United Nations. She was Nigerian Minister of Environment from 2015 to 2016.

Aminata Touré (12 December 1952 – 12 January 2022) was a Guinean politician. She was mayor of Kaloum from 2018 until her death in 2022. Touré died in Morocco from a long illness, on 12 January 2022, at the age of 69.

Amin al-Hafiz (12 November 1921 – 17 December 2009), also known as Amin Hafez, was a Syrian general, politician, and member of the Ba'ath Party. He was the President of Syria from 27 July 1963 to 23 February 1966.

Hakīm Abul-Hasan Yamīn al-Dīn Khusrow Balkhi Dehlavi (1253-1325) or Amir Khosrow was a Persian poet. Amir Khusrow lived in Delhi. His poems are in Persian and Hindi. Allaudin Khilji (1296 A.D - 1316 A.D) had a court minister named Hazrat Amir Khusro who was said to be highly gifted in music with an exceptionally innovative mind. His contribution to Hindustani classical music was said to be unmatched. It is also said that he created the Sitar (probably inspired by the Veena and other string instruments of Persia). The modification of the Pakhawaj into the Tabla is also credited to him. It has also been said that Amir Khusro introduced many styles of singing including Khayal, Tarana, Ghazal and Qawali. He is credited for some most popular Ragas like Yaman, Poorya and Poorvi.

Amiri Baraka (born Everett Leroy Jones; October 7, 1934 – January 9, 2014), previously known as LeRoi Jones, was an American writer. He has written poetry, drama, essays and music criticism. He is also the father of Newark city mayor Ras Baraka. Baraka has been called "one of the most influential and prolific African American writers of the twentieth century." Baraka's poetry and other writing have been both praised and hated. In the African-American community, some compare Baraka to James Baldwin. They see him as one of the most respected and most widely published black writers of his time. Others have said that his work shows much violence, misogyny, and homophobia. Baraka's writings have made controversy over the years, mostly because of his advocacy of rape and violence towards (at many times) women, gay people, white people, and Jews. Critics of his work have said such words are examples of racism, sexism, homophobia, and anti-Semitism in his work. Most American white men are trained to be fags. For this reason it is no wonder their faces are weak and blank.... The average ofay [white person] thinks of the black man as potentially raping every white lady in sight. Which is true, in the sense that the black man should want to rob the white man of everything he has. But for most whites the guilt of the robbery is the guilt of rape. That is, they know in their deepest hearts that they should be robbed, and the white woman understands that only in the rape sequence is she likely to get cleanly, viciously popped. Baraka died January 9, 2014 in Newark, New Jersey after being hospitalized in the facility's intensive care unit for one month prior to his death. He was 79 years old. The cause of death was complications of surgery. Baraka had diabetes. Preface to a Twenty Volume Suicide Note, poems, 1961 Blues Peple: Negro Music in White America, 1963 Raise Race Rays Raize: Essays Since 1965, 1971 The Motion of History and Other Plays, 1978 Daggers and Javelins: Essays 1974-1979, 1984 The Autobiography of LeRoi Jones/Amiri Baraka, 1984 The Music: Reflections on Jazz and Blues, 1987 Transbluesency: The Selected Poems of Amiri Baraka/LeRoi Jones, 1995

Aminul Islam (1973 – April 2012) was a Bangladeshi trade unionist (someone who organises trade unions). He was murdered in 2012. Islam was a former garment worker and was president of the Ashulia and Savar Bangladesh Garment & Industrial Workers Federation. Also he was the leader of Bangladesh Center of Worker Solidarity. It has advocated for improved working conditions and higher wages. In 2010, the organization led protested to push for a larger increase in the minimum wage for garment workers. Islam and other protester were arrested for that. Islam had recently been working to organize workers in factories, which belonged to the Shanta Group. The company produces clothing for multiple American companies, like Tommy Hilfiger, Nike, and Ralph Lauren. He had also assisted ABC News, for an interview with the survivors of a recent factory fire in Bangladesh.

Amir Ohana, Hebrew: אמיר אוחנה, (born 15 March 1976 in Beer Sheba) is an Israeli politician and lawyer. Previously he worked at Shin Bet (internal intelligence agency of Israel). He is the Speaker of the Knesset (Israeli parliament) since 29 December 2022. Ohana has been a Member of the Knesset for Likud since 2015. He is the first openly gay MK for his party. From 2019 to 2020 he was justice minister in the Fourth Netanyahu Government, and from 2020 to 2021 he was minister of internal security in the Fifth Netanyahu Government.
Aminul Islam (1 January 1935 – 29 November 2017) was a Bangladeshi academic. He was the president of Bangladesh Academy of Sciences. He was a fellow of the academy since 1978.

Amintore Fanfani (; 6 February 1908 – 20 November 1999) was an Italian politician. He was the Prime Minister of Italy for five separate times.
